chapters.title: Book 1
paragraphs: 1. From my grandfather Verus I learned good character and control of my temper.
2. From my father's reputation and my memory of him: modesty and a manly character.

3. From my mother: reverence for the gods and generosity; holding back not only from doing wrong, but even from thinking of it; and also a simple way of living, far removed from the habits of the rich.

4. From my great-grandfather: not to have been sent to the public schools open to everyone, but to have had good teachers at home, and to know that on an education like this one should spend generously.

5. From my tutor: not to be a supporter of either the Green or the Blue faction at the races in the Circus, nor a fan of either the Parmularius or the Scutarius, the light-shield and heavy-shield fighters, at the gladiator fights. From him, too, I learned to endure hard work and to want little; to work with my own hands; not to meddle in other people's affairs; and not to be quick to listen to slander.

6. From Diognetus: not to busy myself with trivial things; not to believe what miracle-workers and conjurers say about spells and driving out spirits and things of that kind; not to breed quails for fighting, or get carried away by such pastimes; and to put up with people speaking their minds freely. It was through him, too, that I became at home with philosophy, and heard the lectures first of Bacchius, then of Tandasis and Marcianus; that I wrote dialogues when I was young; and that I wanted a plank bed and an animal skin to sleep on, and whatever else of that kind belongs to the Greek philosophical training.

7. From Rusticus I got the impression that my character needed correcting and training. From him I learned not to be drawn into ambition to shine as a sophist, a showman of clever speeches, nor into writing about abstract theories, nor into delivering little moral sermons, nor into parading myself as a man of strict self-discipline, or as someone who does good deeds for show. I learned from him to keep away from rhetoric, poetry and fancy writing; not to walk around the house in my outdoor clothes, or do other things of that kind; to write my letters plainly, like the letter Rusticus wrote to my mother from Sinuessa; to be easily calmed and reconciled with those who have offended me in words or done me wrong, as soon as they show they are willing to be reconciled; to read carefully, and not be satisfied with a rough grasp of a book; and not to be quick to agree with people who talk too much. And I owe it to him that I came to know the discourses of Epictetus, which he shared with me from his own collection.

8. From Apollonius I learned freedom of will and a firm purpose that does not waver; never, even for a moment, to look to anything but reason; to be always the same—in sharp pain, at the loss of a child, in long illness; to see clearly, in a living example, that the same man can be both very determined and easygoing, and not irritable when teaching; to have had before my eyes a man who plainly regarded his experience and his skill in explaining philosophical principles as the least of his merits; and from him I learned how to accept what are counted as favors from friends, without either being humbled by them or letting them pass unacknowledged.

9. From Sextus: kindliness; the example of a household governed by a father's care; the idea of living in keeping with nature, that is, as nature made a human being to live; dignity without pretense; careful attention to the interests of friends; patience with ignorant people, and with those who form opinions without thinking. He could adapt himself easily to everyone, so that his company was more pleasant than any flattery, and yet those who spent time with him held him in the highest respect. He had the ability to discover the principles we need for living, and to set them in order intelligently and methodically. He never showed anger or any other passion; he was entirely free from passion—from disturbing emotion—and yet full of affection. He could express approval without fuss, and he had great learning without showing it off.

10. From Alexander the grammarian: not to be a fault-finder, and not to scold people who use an uncouth, ungrammatical or odd-sounding expression, but tactfully to bring in the very expression that should have been used—in the course of an answer, or while agreeing with them, or while joining them in looking into the matter itself rather than the word, or by some other fitting hint.

11. From Fronto I learned to notice what envy, deceit and hypocrisy are like in a tyrant; and that, on the whole, those among us who are called Patricians are rather lacking in natural, fatherly affection.

12. From Alexander the Platonist: not to say to anyone, or write in a letter, that I have no time, either often or without real need; and not to keep excusing myself from the duties we owe to the people we live with by pleading urgent business.

13. From Catulus: not to shrug it off when a friend finds fault, even if he finds fault without reason, but to try to bring him back to his usual frame of mind; to be ready to speak well of teachers, as is reported of Domitius and Athenodotus; and to love my children truly.

14. From my brother Severus: to love my family, to love truth, and to love justice. Through him I came to know of Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion and Brutus. From him I received the idea of a state with the same law for everyone, governed on the basis of equal rights and equal freedom of speech, and the idea of a monarchy that respects above all the freedom of those it governs. From him I also learned to value philosophy steadily and consistently; to be ready to do good and quick to give; to stay hopeful; and to trust that my friends love me. I saw in him that he never hid his opinion of those he condemned, and that his friends never had to guess what he wanted or did not want; it was plain.

15. From Maximus I learned self-control, and not to be swayed by anything; to be cheerful in all circumstances, illness included; a character with the right blend of gentleness and dignity; and to do the work in front of me without complaining. I saw that everyone believed he meant what he said, and that whatever he did, he did with no bad intent. He was never astonished or startled, never in a hurry, never put things off; he was never at a loss or downcast; he never laughed to hide his irritation, nor, on the other hand, was he ever quick-tempered or suspicious. He was in the habit of doing kindnesses, ready to forgive, and free from all falsehood. He gave the impression of a man who could not be turned from what was right, rather than of a man who had needed to be set right. I noticed, too, that no one could ever think Maximus looked down on him, or ever venture to think himself the better man. He also had the gift of being pleasantly humorous.

16. In my father I saw gentleness, and unshakable firmness in decisions he had reached after careful thought; no vanity about the things people call honors; a love of work, and persistence; readiness to listen to anyone who had something to propose for the common good; unwavering firmness in giving everyone what he deserved; and the knowledge, gained from experience, of when to act vigorously and when to ease off. I saw that he had overcome all passion for boys; that he thought of himself as no more than any other citizen; that he freed his friends from any obligation to dine with him or to travel with him when he went away; and that those who had been kept from going with him by some urgent business always found him unchanged toward them. I saw how carefully he looked into every matter he had to decide, and how persistently, and that he never cut his inquiry short because he was satisfied with first impressions. I saw that it was his way to keep his friends, neither tiring of them quickly nor being extravagant in his affection; to be content in every situation, and cheerful; to see far ahead, and to take care of the smallest matters without fuss; to put an immediate stop to public applause and all flattery; to keep constant watch over what the government of the empire needed; to manage its spending carefully; and to put up patiently with the criticism he got for doing so. He was not superstitious about the gods, and he did not try to win people over with gifts, or by pleasing them, or by flattering the crowd; he showed moderation and steadiness in everything, never anything petty or base in thought or action, and no craving for novelty. The things that make life comfortable, which fortune supplied him in plenty, he used without arrogance and without apology: when he had them, he enjoyed them without pretense, and when he did not have them, he did not miss them. No one could ever have called him a sophist, or a pert, flippant slave raised in the house, or a pedant; everyone recognized him as a mature and complete man, above flattery, able to manage both his own affairs and other people's. Besides this, he honored those who were true philosophers; he did not scorn those who only pretended to be philosophers, but he was not easily led by them either. He was easy to talk to, and he made himself pleasant without any tiresome affectation. He took reasonable care of his health—not as someone clinging to life, nor out of concern for his looks, nor yet carelessly—so that, thanks to his own attention, he very seldom needed a doctor's skill, or medicines, or ointments. He was very ready, and without envy, to give way to people who had some special ability, such as eloquence, or knowledge of the law or of morals, or of anything else; and he helped them, so that each might have the reputation he deserved. He always acted according to the ancestral customs of his country, without making a show of doing so. Further, he did not like change and was not restless; he liked to stay in the same places and busy himself with the same things. After his attacks of headache he went straight back, fresh and vigorous, to his usual work. He had few secrets—very few, and only rarely—and those only about public matters. He was sensible and sparing in putting on public shows, in constructing public buildings, in his gifts to the people and in things of that kind, for he was a man who looked at what needed to be done, not at the reputation to be gained from doing it. He did not bathe at odd hours; he was not fond of building houses; he was not particular about his food, or about the weave and color of his clothes, or about the good looks of his slaves. His clothes came from Lorium, his villa on the coast, and from Lanuvium generally. We know how he treated the toll-collector at Tusculum who asked his pardon; and all his behavior was like that. There was nothing harsh about him, nothing unforgiving or violent, nothing forced, nothing, as they say, carried to the point of sweating. He examined everything item by item, as if he had all the time in the world—calmly, in an orderly way, vigorously and consistently. What is recorded of Socrates could be said of him: he could do without the things that most people are too weak to do without, and he could enjoy the things that most people cannot enjoy without excess. To be strong enough both to hold out when one lacks such things and to stay sober when one has them is the mark of a man with a perfect and unconquerable soul, such as he showed during the illness of Maximus.

17. To the gods I owe it that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good companions, good relatives and friends—almost everything good. I owe it to the gods, too, that I was never rushed into offending any of the gods, though I had the kind of temperament that, given the chance, might have led me to do something of the sort; but by their favor things never came together in a way that put me to the test. I am grateful to the gods, too, that I was not brought up any longer with my grandfather's mistress; that I kept the freshness of my youth, and did not prove my manhood before the proper time, but even put it off; that I was placed under a ruler and father who could strip all pride from me and bring me to see that a man can live in a palace without needing bodyguards, or embroidered robes, or torches and statues and that kind of show—that such a man can bring himself very close to the way a private citizen lives, without being on that account any less noble in thought or any slacker in action when it comes to doing what must be done for the public good in the way that befits a ruler. I thank the gods that I had such a brother, whose character could rouse me to keep watch over myself, and who at the same time gladdened me with his respect and affection; that my children have been neither dull-witted nor deformed in body; that I did not get further in rhetoric, poetry and the other studies, which might perhaps have taken me over completely if I had seen myself making progress in them; that I was quick to give the people who brought me up the position of honor they seemed to want, instead of putting them off with the hope that I would do it later, on the grounds that they were still young; that I knew Apollonius, Rusticus and Maximus; that I received clear and frequent impressions of what it is to live in keeping with nature, and what kind of life that is—so that, as far as it depended on the gods and their gifts, help and inspiration, nothing stopped me from living in keeping with nature at once, though I still fall short of it through my own fault, and through not heeding the gods' reminders and, I might almost say, their direct instructions; I thank the gods, too, that my body has held out so long in the kind of life I lead; that I never touched either Benedicta or Theodotus, and that, after I did fall into passions of love, I was cured; that though I was often annoyed with Rusticus, I never did anything I had cause to regret; that, although it was my mother's fate to die young, she spent her last years with me; that whenever I wanted to help someone in need, or on any other occasion, I was never told that I did not have the means; and that I myself never fell into the same need, of having to accept anything from someone else; that I have such a wife—so obedient, so affectionate, so unpretentious; that I had plenty of good teachers for my children; that remedies have been shown to me in dreams, both for other ailments and against spitting blood and dizziness...; and that when I became drawn to philosophy I did not fall into the hands of any sophist, and did not waste my time on writers of histories, or on solving logical syllogisms, or on studying the phenomena of the sky. For all these things need the help of the gods and of fortune. Written among the Quadi, on the Granua.

chapters.title: Book 2
paragraphs: 1. Begin each morning by telling yourself: today I shall meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, and careless of others. They are like this because they do not know what is good and what is bad. But I have seen what the good is, and that it is noble; and what the bad is, and that it is shameful. And I have seen what the wrongdoer himself is: he is my kin—not only because we share the same blood or seed, but because we share the same intelligence and the same portion of the divine. So none of them can harm me, since none of them can drag me into anything shameful. Nor can I be angry with my kinsman or hate him. For we were made to work together, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the upper and lower rows of teeth. To work against one another, then, is against nature; and to resent someone and turn away from him is to work against him.

2. Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh, a little breath, and the ruling faculty—the reasoning mind that governs the rest of me. Throw away your books; stop letting yourself be distracted; that is no longer allowed. Instead, as though you were already dying, think nothing of the flesh: it is blood and bones and a network, a woven tangle of nerves, veins and arteries. Look at the breath too, and see what it is: air, and never the same air, but every moment breathed out and drawn in again. The third part, then, is the ruling faculty. Consider this: you are an old man, so do not let this part be a slave any longer. Do not let it be jerked on strings like a puppet by impulses that set you against others. Do not let it be discontented any longer with what you have been given now, or shrink from what is to come.

3. Everything that comes from the gods is full of providence—the gods' care and foresight. Even what comes from fortune is not separate from nature; it is woven and bound together with the things that providence directs. Everything flows from providence. Necessity plays its part too, and so does what benefits the whole universe, of which you are a part. Whatever the nature of the universe brings about, and whatever keeps that nature in being, is good for every part of nature. And the universe is kept in being by change: by the changes of the elements, and equally by the changes of the things made from the elements. Let these principles be enough for you; hold them always as settled judgments. But throw away your thirst for books, so that you do not die grumbling, but cheerfully, sincerely, and grateful to the gods from your heart.

4. Remember how long you have been putting all this off, and how many times the gods have given you an opportunity that you have not used. It is time now, at last, to understand what universe you are a part of, and who governs that universe—the one from whom your own existence flows. Understand, too, that a limit has been set to your time. If you do not use it to clear the clouds from your mind, it will pass, and you will pass, and it will never come back.

5. Every moment, set your mind firmly, as a Roman and a man, on doing the task in front of you with complete and unpretentious dignity, with warmth, freedom and justice. And set it on freeing yourself from every other thought. You will free yourself if you do each act of your life as if it were your last: without carelessness, without the passionate aversion that turns away from what reason commands, without pretense, without self-love, and without discontent with the share you have been given. You see how few things there are: whoever holds on to them is able to live a life that flows quietly, like the life of the gods. For the gods, on their part, will ask nothing more of someone who keeps to these things.

6. Go on, keep wronging yourself, my soul, keep wronging yourself! But you will no longer have the chance to honor yourself. Each person's life is enough; but yours is nearly over, and still you do not respect yourself, but make your happiness depend on the souls of others.

7. Do the things that happen to you from outside distract you? Then give yourself time to learn something new and good, and stop being spun around. But you must also guard against being carried off in the other direction. For some people wear themselves out with activity all their lives, yet have no goal toward which to direct every impulse and, in short, every thought; and they too are wasting their lives on trifles.
8. People are seldom made unhappy by failing to notice what goes on in someone else's mind; but those who do not pay attention to the movements of their own minds are bound to be unhappy.

9. Always keep this in mind: what the nature of the whole is, and what my own nature is; how the one is related to the other; and what kind of part mine is, and of what kind of whole. And remember that no one can stop you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part.

10. Theophrastus, comparing wrong acts as one would compare them by ordinary human standards, says, like a true philosopher, that wrongs done out of desire deserve more blame than wrongs done out of anger. For someone who is gripped by anger seems to turn away from reason with a kind of pain, and a shrinking inside that he is not aware of. But someone who does wrong out of desire, overcome by pleasure, seems in a way more self-indulgent and more womanish in his wrongdoing. So he was right, and spoke as a philosopher should, when he said that a wrong done with pleasure deserves more blame than one done with pain. In general, the angry person is more like someone who has first been wronged and is driven to anger by the pain of it; the other has set out to do wrong on his own impulse, carried into the act by desire.

11. Since you may leave life at any moment, let that thought govern everything you do and think. If there are gods, leaving the company of human beings is nothing to fear, for the gods would not involve you in anything bad. And if there are no gods, or if they do not care about human affairs, why should I want to live in a universe without gods, or without providence? But in fact they do exist, and they do care about human affairs, and they have put it entirely in a person's power not to fall into what is truly bad. As for everything else, if any of it were bad, they would have provided for that too, so that it would be entirely in a person's power not to fall into it. And how can something that does not make a person worse make that person's life worse? If such things were bad, the nature of the universe could not have let them slip past it—not from ignorance, and not from knowing about them but lacking the power to prevent or correct them. Nor could it have made so great a mistake, through lack of power or lack of skill, that good and bad things would fall without distinction on good people and bad. Yet death and life, honor and dishonor, pain and pleasure all happen equally to good people and bad, and they make us neither better nor worse. Therefore they are neither good nor bad.

12. How quickly everything vanishes: the bodies themselves vanish into the universe, and even the memory of them vanishes into time. Consider what all the things the senses perceive really are—especially those that lure us with the bait of pleasure, or frighten us with pain, or are made famous by empty reputation—how worthless, contemptible, dirty, perishable and dead they are. It is the work of our power of understanding to observe this. It should observe, too, who these people are whose opinions and voices make a reputation. And it should observe what death is: if a person looks at death by itself, and by the power of thought takes apart everything the imagination has attached to it, he will see that it is nothing but a process of nature; and anyone who is afraid of a process of nature is a child. Yet death is not only a process of nature; it also serves nature's purposes. And it should observe how a human being comes near to God, through what part of himself he does so, and in what condition that part is when he does.

13. Nothing is more wretched than a person who runs around in circles after everything, and pries into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and tries to guess what is going on in his neighbors' minds, without realizing that it is enough to attend to the divine spirit within him—the guiding mind that is his share of the divine—and to honor it sincerely. And honoring it means keeping it pure from passion, from thoughtlessness, and from discontent with what comes from gods and human beings. For what comes from the gods deserves reverence because of its excellence. What comes from human beings should be dear to us because we are kin; and sometimes, in a way, it even moves our pity, because people do not know good from bad—a blindness no less serious than the one that leaves us unable to tell white from black.

14. Even if you were going to live three thousand years, or ten thousand times that, still remember that no one loses any life except the one he is living now, and no one lives any life except the one he is losing. So the longest life and the shortest come to the same thing. For the present moment is the same for everyone, even though the time that has passed away is not the same for all; and so what is lost turns out to be a mere moment. No one can lose the past or the future: how could anyone take from a person what he does not have? So you must keep these two things in mind. First, that all things have had the same forms from eternity and come round again in a circle, and that it makes no difference whether a person watches the same things for a hundred years, or two hundred, or for endless time. Second, that the person who lives longest and the person who dies soonest lose exactly the same. For the present is the only thing anyone can be deprived of—if it is true that it is the only thing he has, and that no one can lose what he does not have.

15. Remember that everything is opinion—what we judge things to be. For what the Cynic Monimus said is plain; and plain too is how useful his saying is, if you take from it what it has to offer, as far as it is true.

16. The human soul does violence to itself, first of all, when it becomes, as far as it can, an abscess, a kind of tumor on the universe. For to resent anything that happens is to break away from nature, which holds within it, each in its part, the natures of all other things. Second, the soul does violence to itself when it turns away from another person, or even goes at him meaning to harm him, as the souls of angry people do. Third, when it is overcome by pleasure or by pain. Fourth, when it puts on an act, and does or says anything falsely or insincerely. Fifth, when it lets any act or impulse of its own go without an aim, and does anything thoughtlessly, without considering what it is doing. For even the smallest things ought to be done for a purpose; and the purpose of rational beings is to follow the reason and the law of the oldest city and commonwealth of all—the universe itself.

17. In human life, time is a point; the stuff we are made of is always flowing; our perception is dim; the whole body, as it is put together, is prone to rot; the soul is a whirl; fortune is hard to predict; and fame has no judgment. In a word, everything belonging to the body is a river, and everything belonging to the soul is a dream and a vapor; life is a war and a stay in a foreign land; and after fame comes oblivion. What, then, can guide a person through it? One thing, and only one: philosophy. And philosophy means keeping the divine spirit within a person safe from violence and harm, stronger than pains and pleasures; doing nothing without a purpose, and nothing falsely or hypocritically; not needing anyone else to do or not do anything; accepting everything that happens and everything that is given to him as coming from the same source he himself came from, wherever that source may be; and, finally, waiting for death with a cheerful mind, since death is nothing but the breaking up of the elements that every living being is made of. And if the elements themselves come to no harm in constantly changing into one another, why should anyone fear the change and breaking up of all of them? It is in keeping with nature, and nothing that is in keeping with nature is bad. Written at Carnuntum.

chapters.title: Book 3
paragraphs: 1. We ought to consider not only that our life is wasting away day by day, and that less of it is left, but something else as well. If a person lives longer, it is quite uncertain whether his understanding will still be equal to grasping things, and whether it will keep the power of contemplation that strives for knowledge of the divine and the human. For if he begins to slide into senility, he will not stop perspiring and taking nourishment, or having imagination and appetite, or anything else of that kind. But other powers have already been snuffed out: the power to make proper use of ourselves, to fulfil the full measure of our duty, to sort out clearly everything that appears to us, to consider whether it is now time for a person to leave life, and every other power of that kind that absolutely requires a trained reason. So we must hurry, not only because every day brings us nearer to death, but also because our grasp and understanding of things is the first thing to fail.

2. We ought to notice, too, that even the things that come about as side effects of what nature produces have something pleasing and attractive about them. For instance, when bread is baked, some parts split open at the surface. These cracks take a shape that goes against what the baker's art intended, yet in a way they are beautiful, and they have their own particular way of making us want to eat. Again, figs split open when they are fully ripe; and in ripe olives, the very fact that they are close to rotting gives the fruit a beauty of its own. The ears of grain bending down, the lion's brow, the foam that flows from the mouths of wild boars, and many other things are far from beautiful if you look at them one by one. Still, because these side effects follow from things that nature forms, they help to adorn those things, and they please the mind. So if a person has a feeling for the things produced in the universe, and a deeper insight into them, there is hardly one of these side effects that will not seem to him arranged, in its own way, to give pleasure. He will look at the real gaping jaws of wild beasts with no less pleasure than at the ones painters and sculptors imitate. In an old woman or an old man he will be able to see a certain ripeness and grace; and he will be able to look at the attractive loveliness of the young with chaste eyes. Many such things will present themselves. They do not please everyone, but only the person who has become truly familiar with nature and her works.

3. Hippocrates cured many diseases, then fell sick himself and died. The Chaldaeans foretold the deaths of many people, and then fate caught them too. Alexander, Pompeius and Caius Caesar so often destroyed whole cities completely, and cut to pieces many tens of thousands of cavalry and infantry in battle; yet in the end they too left life. Heraclitus speculated so much about the universe ending in fire, and then he was filled with water inside and died smeared all over with mud. Lice destroyed Democritus; and lice of another kind killed Socrates. What does all this mean? You have gone on board, you have made the voyage, you have come to shore: get out. If you are landing in another life, there is no lack of gods even there. But if it is to a state without sensation, you will no longer be held by pains and pleasures, and you will stop being a slave to the vessel, the body. And the vessel is as far below the part of you that serves it as that servant is above it: for the servant is intelligence and the divine, and the vessel is earth and decay.

4. Do not waste what is left of your life in thoughts about other people, when you are not relating those thoughts to something that serves the common good. For when you have such thoughts, you lose the chance to do something else. Thoughts like these: What is so-and-so doing, and why? What is he saying? What is he thinking about? What is he scheming? These, and everything else of the kind, make us wander away from watching over our own ruling faculty. So in the chain of our thoughts we ought to hold back everything that is aimless and useless, and most of all whatever is over-curious or malicious. A person should train himself to think only about things of this sort: if someone suddenly asked, "What are you thinking about right now?", you could answer at once and with complete openness, "This" or "That." Then it would be plain from your words that everything in you is simple and kind, as befits a being made for community; that you do not care at all for thoughts of pleasure or sensual enjoyment; and that you have no rivalry, envy or suspicion, or anything else you would blush to admit was in your mind. For someone like this, who no longer puts off taking his place among the best, is a kind of priest and servant of the gods. He also makes use of the divine spirit planted within him, which keeps him unstained by pleasure, unharmed by any pain, untouched by any insult, and unable to feel wronged. It makes him a fighter in the noblest of fights, one whom no passion can overpower, dyed deep with justice, welcoming with all his soul everything that happens and is given to him as his share. Only rarely, and only when it is really necessary and for the common good, does he imagine what someone else is saying or doing or thinking. For he makes only what belongs to himself the material of his activity. He keeps constantly in mind the share that has been allotted to him out of the whole sum of things. He makes his own acts noble, and he is convinced that his own portion is good. For the lot assigned to each person is carried along with him, and carries him along with it. He remembers, too, that every rational being is his kin, and that caring for all human beings is in keeping with human nature. Yet a person should care about the opinion not of everyone, but only of those who clearly live in keeping with nature. As for those who do not live that way, he always bears in mind what sort of people they are, at home and away from home, by night and by day; what they are; and with what sort of people they live their impure lives. So he places no value at all on praise from such people, since they are not even satisfied with themselves.

5. Do not work unwillingly, or without regard for the common good, or without proper thought, or while your attention is pulled in different directions. Do not dress up your thoughts in fancy language. Do not be a person of many words, or one who is busy with too many things. Further, let the divine spirit within you be the guardian of a living being who is manly and mature, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler. Let him be someone who has taken up his post like a person waiting for the signal that calls him out of life: ready to go, needing no oath to bind him and no one's testimony to vouch for him. Be cheerful, too, and do not look for help from outside, or for the calm that other people give. A person must stand upright, then, not be held upright by others.

6. Suppose you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control and courage. Suppose, in a word, you find anything better than your own mind being content with itself: content in the things it lets you do according to right reason, and content with the condition assigned to you without your choosing. If, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with all your soul, and enjoy what you have found to be the best. But suppose nothing appears better than the divine spirit planted in you: the spirit that has brought all your impulses under its control, that carefully examines every impression, that, as Socrates said, has pulled itself away from the persuasions of the senses, that has submitted itself to the gods, and that cares for human beings. If you find everything else smaller and of less worth than this, give room to nothing else. For once you turn aside and lean toward something else, you will no longer be able, without being torn, to give first place to the good that properly belongs to you and is your own. For it is not right for anything of a different kind—such as praise from the crowd, or power, or the enjoyment of pleasure—to compete with what is good for a rational being and a member of the community. All these things, even if they seem to fit in with the better things to a small degree, suddenly take the upper hand and carry us away. But you, I say, simply and freely choose what is better, and hold on to it. "But what is useful is better." Very well: if it is useful to you as a rational being, keep to it. But if it is useful to you only as an animal, say so, and keep to your judgment without arrogance. Only make sure that you examine the question by a sound method.

7. Never value anything as being to your advantage if it will force you to break your word, to lose your self-respect, to hate anyone, to suspect, to curse, to be a hypocrite, or to want anything that needs walls and curtains to hide it. For someone who has put his own intelligence, the divine spirit within him, and the worship of its excellence, before everything else does not put on a tragic act, does not groan, and will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Most important of all, he will live without either chasing death or running from it. Whether his soul is to be held within his body for a longer time or a shorter one, he does not care at all. Even if he must leave at once, he will go as readily as if he were going to do anything else that can be done with decency and order. All through life he takes care of this one thing only: that his thoughts never turn away from anything that belongs to an intelligent being and a member of a civic community.

8. In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and purified you will find nothing festering, nothing foul, no sore that has skinned over. Nor is his life left unfinished when fate overtakes him, as one might say of an actor who leaves the stage before the play has reached its end and is complete. Besides, there is nothing in him slavish or pretentious; nothing too tightly bound to other things, and nothing cut off from them; nothing that deserves blame; nothing that looks for a hiding place.

9. Revere your power of forming opinions. It depends entirely on this power whether your ruling faculty will hold any opinion that is out of keeping with nature and with the makeup of a rational being. And this power promises freedom from hasty judgment, friendship toward human beings, and obedience to the gods.

10. Throw everything else away, then, and hold on to these few things only. And remember, too, that each person lives only this present moment, which is an indivisible point; all the rest of his life is either already past or uncertain. Short, then, is the time each person lives; small is the corner of the earth where he lives; and short, too, is even the longest fame after death. And even that fame is kept going only by a succession of poor human beings who will very soon die, and who do not know even themselves, much less someone who died long ago.

11. To the aids already mentioned, add this one more. Make for yourself a definition or description of whatever presents itself to you, so that you see clearly what kind of thing it is in its substance: stripped bare, whole and entire. Tell yourself its proper name, and the names of the parts it was made from and will break back into. For nothing so lifts up the mind as being able to examine, methodically and truthfully, every object that comes before you in life, and always looking at things in such a way as to see at the same time what kind of universe this is; what use each thing serves in it; what value each thing has in relation to the whole, and what value in relation to a human being, who is a citizen of the highest city, of which all other cities are like households. It lifts the mind, too, to see what each thing is, what it is made of, how long this thing that is now making an impression on me is in its nature to last, and what virtue I need in dealing with it: gentleness, manly courage, truthfulness, faithfulness, simplicity, contentment and the rest. So on every occasion a person should say: This comes from God. This comes by the allotting and spinning of the thread of destiny, and by coincidences and chances of that sort. And this comes from someone of my own stock, my kinsman and partner, who does not know, however, what is in keeping with his nature. But I know. So I treat him with kindness and justice, as the natural law of fellowship requires. At the same time, in things that are indifferent—neither good nor bad in themselves—I try to work out the value of each.

12. Do the work in front of you by following right reason seriously, energetically and calmly, not letting anything else distract you, and keeping your divine part pure, as if you had to give it back at once. Hold to this, expecting nothing and fearing nothing, content with acting now in keeping with nature and with speaking heroic truth in every word and sound you utter. If you do, you will live happily. And there is no one who can stop you.

13. Doctors always keep their instruments and knives at hand for cases that suddenly call for their skill. In the same way, keep your principles ready for understanding things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest thing, mindful of the bond that joins the divine and the human to each other. For you will never do anything well in human affairs without relating it at the same time to the divine; nor the other way round.

14. Stop wandering aimlessly. You are not going to read your own memoirs, or the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks, or the passages from books that you were saving for your old age. Hurry on, then, toward the end that lies before you. Throw away empty hopes, and come to your own rescue while you still can, if you care for yourself at all.

15. People do not know how many different things are meant by the words "stealing," "sowing," "buying," "keeping quiet," and "seeing what ought to be done." For that last kind of seeing is not done with the eyes, but with another kind of sight.

16. Body, soul, intelligence. To the body belong sensations; to the soul, impulses; to the intelligence, principles. To receive the stamp of impressions from the way things appear belongs even to animals. To be jerked on the strings of desire belongs to wild beasts, to men who have made themselves womanish, and to a Phalaris or a Nero. And to have intelligence as a guide to what seems fitting belongs also to people who do not believe in the gods, who betray their country, and who do their impure deeds once they have shut the doors. If, then, everything else is shared by all those I have mentioned, what remains that is special to the good person is this: to be pleased and content with what happens and with the thread that is spun for him. It also means not defiling the divine spirit planted in his breast, or disturbing it with a crowd of images, but keeping it at peace, following it obediently as a god, saying nothing contrary to the truth and doing nothing contrary to justice. And if everyone refuses to believe that he lives a simple, modest and contented life, he is not angry with any of them. Nor does he turn aside from the road that leads to the end of life, where a person ought to arrive pure, at peace, ready to leave, and perfectly reconciled to his lot without any compulsion.

chapters.title: Book 4
paragraphs: 1. When the ruling faculty is in keeping with nature, it meets whatever happens in such a way that it always adapts itself easily to what is possible and to what is put before it. For it does not demand any fixed material to work on. It moves toward its purpose, but not unconditionally; and it turns whatever stands in its way into material for itself. It is like a fire that takes hold of whatever falls into it. A small flame would have been put out by these things; but when the fire is strong, it quickly makes whatever is heaped on it its own, burns it up, and rises higher by means of that very material.
2. Let nothing you do be done without a purpose, or in any way other than by the principles that bring a craft to perfection.

3. People look for places to get away to: houses in the country, the seashore, the mountains. And you too are in the habit of longing very much for such things. But this is entirely the mark of the most ordinary sort of person, since it is in your power, whenever you choose, to withdraw into yourself. For there is nowhere a person can withdraw to with more quiet or more freedom from trouble than into his own soul—especially if he has thoughts within him such that, by looking into them, he is at once perfectly calm. And I say that calm is nothing other than a mind in good order. So give yourself this retreat constantly, and renew yourself. Let your principles be brief and basic, so that as soon as you turn to them they will be enough to wash the soul completely clean, and to send you back free of all discontent with the things you are returning to. For what are you discontented with? The badness of people? Call to mind this conclusion: that rational beings exist for one another; that bearing with others is part of justice; and that people do wrong against their will. And think how many people already, after mutual hostility, suspicion, hatred and fighting, have been laid out dead and turned to ashes. And be quiet at last. But perhaps you are discontented with what the universe has allotted you. Then call to mind this alternative: either there is providence, or there are only atoms—things thrown together by chance. Or remember the arguments that have proved that the world is a kind of community of citizens. And be quiet at last. But perhaps the things of the body will still take hold of you. Then consider further that the mind, once it has drawn itself apart and recognized its own power, does not mix with the breath, the life-breath of the body, whether that breath moves gently or roughly. And think, too, of everything you have heard about pain and pleasure and have agreed to. And be quiet at last. But perhaps the craving for what is called fame will torment you. Then see how quickly everything is forgotten. Look at the chaos of endless time on either side of the present; at how empty applause is; at how changeable and lacking in judgment are those who make a show of praising; and at how narrow the space is within which fame is confined. And be quiet at last. For the whole earth is a point, and your home is a tiny corner of it; and how few people live there, and what sort of people they are who will praise you! What remains, then, is this: remember to withdraw into this little territory of your own. Above all, do not pull yourself this way and that, or strain yourself, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal. And among the things you keep closest to hand and turn to, let there be these two. The first is that things do not touch the soul: they stand outside it, motionless, and our disturbances come only from the opinion within. The second is that all these things you see will change in a moment and will no longer be; and keep constantly in mind how many such changes you have already seen for yourself. The universe is change; life is opinion.

4. If the power of thought is common to us all, then reason too, which makes us rational beings, is common to us all. If so, then the reason that commands us what to do and what not to do is also common. If so, there is also a common law. If so, we are fellow citizens. If so, we are members of some community of citizens. If so, the world is in a way a state. For what other shared community could anyone say the whole human race belongs to? And it is from there, from this shared community, that we get our very power of thought, our power of reasoning and our capacity for law—or where else do they come from? For just as the earthly part of me is a portion given to me from earth somewhere, and the watery part from another element, and the hot and fiery part from some source of its own (for nothing comes out of nothing, just as nothing returns into nothing), so the thinking part too comes from some source.

5. Death, like birth, is a mystery of nature: a coming together of the same elements, and a coming apart into the same elements. And it is not at all something anyone should be ashamed of. For it is not against the nature of a rational being, and not against the reason that is part of our makeup.

6. It is natural that people like this should act like this; it is a matter of necessity. Anyone who refuses to accept this is refusing to let the fig tree have its sap. But above all remember this: in a very short time both you and the person who acts like this will be dead, and soon not even your names will be left behind.
7. Take away your opinion, and the complaint "I have been harmed" is taken away. Take away the complaint "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
8. What does not make a person worse than he was does not make his life worse either, and does not harm him, from outside or from within.
9. The nature of what benefits all had no choice but to do this.

10. Consider that everything that happens, happens justly; if you watch carefully, you will find that it is so. I do not mean only that things follow one another in an unbroken order. I mean that they happen justly, as if done by someone who gives each thing what it is worth. So go on watching, as you have begun. And whatever you do, do it while being good—good in the true sense in which a person is understood to be good. Keep to this in every action.
11. Do not take the view of things that the person who wrongs you takes, or the view he wants you to take. Look at them as they truly are.

12. A person should always have these two rules ready. The first is to do only what reason suggests for the good of human beings—the reason of your ruling and law-giving faculty. The second is to change your opinion, if someone is at hand to set you right and move you away from some opinion. But this change of opinion must come only from being persuaded of something, such as that it is just or for the common good, or the like—not because it seems pleasant or brings you a good name.
13. Do you have reason? I do.—Then why do you not use it? For if it is doing its own work, what else do you want?
14. You have existed as a part. You will vanish into what produced you; or rather, you will be changed and taken back into the generative principle of what produced you.
15. Many grains of frankincense on the same altar: one falls sooner, another later; but it makes no difference.
16. Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people who now think you a beast and an ape—if you go back to your principles and to your reverence for reason.
17. Do not act as if you were going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over you. While you live, while it is in your power, be good.

18. How much trouble a person spares himself when he does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only at what he does himself, so that it may be just and pure! Or, as Agathon says, do not look around at the corrupt ways of others, but run straight along the line without swerving from it.

19. Someone who has a burning desire for fame after death does not consider that every one of those who remember him will very soon die too; and then, in turn, those who come after them; until the whole memory of him has been snuffed out, as it is passed along through people who foolishly admire and then perish. But suppose that those who will remember you were even immortal, and that the memory would be immortal: what is that to you? And I do not mean, what is it to the dead? I mean, what is it to the living? What is praise, except, of course, insofar as it has some practical use? For as it is, you are rejecting nature's gift out of season, and clinging to something else....

20. Everything that is beautiful in any way is beautiful in itself, and its beauty ends there, in itself; praise is no part of it. So a thing is made neither worse nor better by being praised. I say this also of the things that ordinary people call beautiful, such as material objects and works of art. What is truly beautiful needs nothing further—no more than law does, no more than truth, no more than kindness or modesty. Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or spoiled because it is blamed? Is an emerald made worse than it was if it is not praised? Or gold, ivory, purple cloth, a lyre, a little knife, a flower, a shrub?

21. If souls go on existing, how does the air hold them all from eternity?—But how does the earth hold the bodies of those who have been buried for so many ages? Here on earth, after these bodies have lasted for a certain time, whatever it may be, they change and break up, and so make room for other dead bodies. In the same way, the souls that move into the air last for some time, and then they are changed and spread out, and take on a fiery nature as they are taken back into the generative intelligence of the universe. In this way they make room for the new souls that come to live there. This is the answer one might give on the assumption that souls go on existing. But we must think not only of the number of bodies that are buried in this way, but also of the number of animals that are eaten every day by us and by other animals. What a number is consumed, and so in a way buried in the bodies of those who feed on them! And yet the earth holds them, because these bodies are changed into blood and transformed into air or fire. How is the truth of this matter to be investigated? By dividing things into what is material and what is the cause that gives them form.
22. Do not let yourself be tossed about. In every impulse, hold to what is just; and with every impression, keep hold of your power to grasp and understand it.

23. Everything that is in harmony with you, O Universe, is in harmony with me. Nothing that comes at the right time for you is too early or too late for me. Everything your seasons bring, O Nature, is fruit to me. From you are all things, in you are all things, to you all things return. The poet says of Athens, "Dear city of Cecrops"; and will you not say, "Dear city of Zeus"?

24. "Do few things," says the philosopher, "if you want to be calm." But consider whether it would not be better to say: Do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a being made by nature for community requires, and in the way that reason requires it. For this brings not only the calm that comes from doing things well, but also the calm that comes from doing few things. Most of what we say and do is unnecessary; if a person cuts it away, he will have more leisure and less unease. So on every occasion a person should ask himself: Is this one of the unnecessary things? And he should cut away not only unnecessary acts but also unnecessary thoughts; for then unnecessary acts will not follow after them.
25. Try living the life of the good person, and see how it suits you: the life of someone who is content with his share of the whole, and content with his own just acts and kindly disposition.

26. Have you seen those things? Now look at these too. Do not trouble yourself. Make yourself wholly simple. Is someone doing wrong? It is himself he wrongs. Has something happened to you? Very well. Everything that happens was allotted to you and spun out for you from the universe from the beginning. In a word: your life is short. You must make good use of the present, with the help of reason and justice. Be sober even when you relax.

27. Either the universe is well ordered, or it is a chaos thrown together—but even so, a universe. But can there be some order in you, and disorder in the whole? And that, too, when all things are so distinct from one another, so spread through the whole, and so bound together in sympathy, each affecting the others?
28. A dark character, a womanish character, a stubborn character; bestial, childish, brutish, stupid, fake, coarse and jeering, cheating, tyrannical.

29. If someone who does not know what is in the universe is a stranger to it, someone who does not know what is happening in it is no less a stranger. Whoever flees from the reason that makes us a community is a runaway. Whoever shuts the eyes of his understanding is blind. Whoever needs someone else, and does not have within himself everything that is useful for life, is poor. Whoever withdraws and cuts himself off from the reason of our common nature, because he is displeased with what happens, is an abscess on the universe—for the same nature that brings this about brought you about too. Whoever tears his own soul away from the soul of rational beings, which is one, is a piece torn off from the state.

30. One is a philosopher without a tunic, another without a book; here is another, half-naked. "I have no bread," he says, "and I hold fast to reason." And I, for my part, get no living from my learning, and I hold fast to my reason.

31. Love the craft you have learned, however humble it may be, and be content with it. And go through the rest of your life as someone who has entrusted everything he has to the gods with his whole soul, making yourself neither a tyrant nor a slave to anyone.

32. Think, for example, of the times of Vespasian. You will see all the same things: people marrying, raising children, falling sick, dying, waging war, feasting, trading, farming the land, flattering, being stubbornly arrogant, suspecting, plotting, wishing for some to die, grumbling at the present, loving, piling up treasure, longing for the consulship, for royal power. Well, that life of theirs no longer exists anywhere. Move on again to the times of Trajan. Again, everything is the same. Their life too is gone. Look in the same way at the other periods of time and of whole nations, and see how many, after great efforts, soon fell and were broken up into the elements. But above all, think of the people you yourself have known who let themselves be pulled this way and that by empty things, and neglected to do what was in keeping with their own makeup, and to hold fast to it and be content with it. And here you must remember that the attention given to each thing has its own proper value and proportion. For then you will not become dissatisfied, as long as you give smaller matters no more attention than is fitting.

33. Words that were once in common use are now out of date. So too the names of those who were once famous are now, in a way, out of date: Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Leonnatus; and a little later Scipio and Cato too; then Augustus; then Hadrianus and Antoninus as well. For all things soon fade and become a mere story, and complete oblivion soon buries them. And I say this of those who shone in some wonderful way. As for the rest, as soon as they have breathed their last they are gone, and no one speaks of them. And, to sum up, even everlasting remembrance—what is it? Nothing at all. What, then, should we give our serious effort to? This one thing: just thoughts, acts that serve the community, words that never lie, and a disposition that gladly accepts everything that happens as necessary, as familiar, as flowing from a source and origin of the same kind.
34. Give yourself up willingly to Clotho, one of the Fates, and let her spin your thread into whatever she pleases.
35. Everything lasts only a day, both what remembers and what is remembered.

36. Watch constantly how all things come about through change, and train yourself to see that the nature of the universe loves nothing so much as to change the things that exist and to make new things like them. For everything that exists is, in a way, the seed of what will be. But you think only of seeds that are sown in the earth or in a womb; and that is a very crude idea.

37. You will soon die, and you are not yet simple, not yet free from disturbance, not yet free from the suspicion that things outside you can harm you, not yet kind to everyone; nor do you yet hold that wisdom lies in acting justly and in that alone.
38. Look into people's ruling faculties, even those of the wise, and see what sort of things they avoid and what sort of things they pursue.

39. What is bad for you does not lie in someone else's ruling faculty, nor in any shift or change of the body that covers you. Where is it, then? It lies in that part of you which has the power to form opinions about what is bad. So let that power not form such opinions, and all is well. And even if the thing nearest to it, your poor body, is cut, burned, full of pus and rot, still let the part that forms opinions about these things stay quiet. That is, let it judge that nothing that can happen equally to a bad person and a good one is either bad or good. For what happens equally to someone who lives against nature and to someone who lives in keeping with nature is neither in keeping with nature nor against it.

40. Always think of the universe as one living being, with one substance and one soul. Notice how everything is brought back to one perception, the perception of this one living being; how everything acts by one impulse; and how all things work together as causes of everything that exists. Notice, too, how the thread is spun without a break, and how the web is woven together.
41. You are a little soul carrying a corpse around, as Epictetus used to say.
42. It is nothing bad for things to undergo change, and nothing good for things to exist as a result of change.
43. Time is like a river made of the things that happen—a violent current. As soon as each thing has been seen, it is swept away, and another comes in its place, and that too will be swept away.

44. Everything that happens is as familiar and well known as the rose in spring and fruit in summer. So it is with disease, death, slander, treachery, and whatever else delights fools or troubles them.

45. In the chain of things, what comes after always fits what went before. For this chain is not like a mere list of unconnected things, joined only because one must follow another; it is a rational connection. And just as all existing things are arranged together in harmony, so the things that come into being show not mere succession, but a wonderful kinship.

46. Always remember what Heraclitus said: that the death of earth is to become water, the death of water is to become air, the death of air is to become fire, and so back again. Think too of the person who forgets where the road leads. Think too how people quarrel with the very thing they are most constantly in touch with, the reason that governs the universe; and that the things they meet every day seem strange to them. And consider that we ought not to act and speak as if we were asleep, for even in sleep we seem to act and speak; and that we ought not, like children taught by their parents, simply to act and speak as we have been taught.

47. If some god told you that you would die tomorrow, or at the latest the day after, you would not much care whether it was the day after or tomorrow—unless you were utterly small-minded. For how small the difference is! In the same way, do not think it matters much whether you die tomorrow or after as many years as you can name.

48. Think constantly of how many doctors have died after frowning so often over the sick; how many astrologers, after grandly predicting other people's deaths; how many philosophers, after endless discussions about death or immortality; how many heroes, after killing thousands; how many tyrants, after using their power over people's lives with terrible arrogance, as if they themselves were immortal; and how many whole cities have, so to speak, died—Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others. Add to the count all the people you yourself have known, one after another. One man buried another and was then laid out dead himself, and someone else buried him—and all this in a short time. In short, always see how short-lived and worthless human things are: what was yesterday a little mucus will tomorrow be a mummy or ashes. So pass through this little stretch of time in keeping with nature, and end your journey content, as an olive falls when it is ripe, blessing nature, who produced it, and thanking the tree on which it grew.

49. Be like the headland that the waves keep breaking against: it stands firm, and tames the raging water around it. "Am I unhappy because this has happened to me?" Not at all. Rather: "I am happy, even though this has happened to me, because I remain free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor afraid of the future." For something like this could have happened to anyone; but not everyone would have remained free from pain when it did. Why, then, call what happened a misfortune, rather than call your remaining free from pain a good fortune? Do you, in general, call something a person's misfortune when it is not a departure from human nature? And does something seem to you a departure from human nature when it is not against what human nature wills? Well, you know what nature wills. Will what has happened, then, stop you from being just, great-souled, self-controlled, sensible, guarded against rash opinions and falsehood? Will it stop you from having modesty, freedom and all the rest—the qualities whose presence gives human nature everything that is its own? Remember too, whenever something leads you toward vexation, to apply this principle: not "this is a misfortune," but "to bear this nobly is good fortune."

50. It is an ordinary kind of help, but still a useful one, toward thinking little of death, to call to mind people who clung hard to life. What more did they gain than those who died early? In the end, surely, they lie in their graves somewhere—Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus, or anyone else like them, who carried many others out to burial and then were carried out themselves. Altogether, the span between birth and death is small; and think how laboriously that span is lived through: with how much trouble, in the company of what sort of people, and in how feeble a body. So do not regard life as a thing of any value. For look at the vast stretch of time behind you, and at the time ahead of you, another boundless expanse. In this infinity, what difference is there between one who lives three days and one who lives three generations?

51. Always run by the short road; and the short road is the natural one. So say and do everything in keeping with the soundest reason. For a purpose like this frees a person from trouble and warfare, and from all scheming and showy display.

chapters.title: Book 5
paragraphs: 1. In the morning, when you are reluctant to get up, keep this thought ready: I am getting up to do the work of a human being. Why, then, am I discontented, if I am going to do the things I exist for, the things I was brought into the world to do? Or was I made for this: to lie under the blankets and keep myself warm?—But this is more pleasant.—Do you exist, then, for pleasure, and not at all for action and effort? Do you not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders and the bees, all working together, each putting in order its own part of the universe? And are you unwilling to do the work of a human being? Do you not hurry to do what is in keeping with your nature?—But one must rest too.—One must. But nature has set limits to this as well, just as she has set limits to eating and drinking. Yet you go beyond these limits, beyond what is enough, while in your actions you do not: you stop short of what you could do. So you do not love yourself. If you did, you would love your nature and what she wills. Those who love their own crafts wear themselves out working at them, unwashed and unfed. But you value your own nature less than the wood-turner values his turning, or the dancer his dancing, or the money-lover his money, or the vain man his bit of glory. When such people are gripped by a passion for something, they would rather go without food and sleep than stop working to perfect what they care about. Are the acts that serve the community worth less in your eyes, and less deserving of your effort?
2. How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troubling or out of place, and at once to be completely calm.

3. Judge worthy of you every word and every act that is in keeping with nature. Do not let yourself be turned aside by the criticism that may come from some people afterward, or by their talk. If something is good to do or to say, do not think it beneath you. Those people have their own ruling faculty and follow their own impulses. Pay no attention to that. Go straight on, following your own nature and the nature of the universe; and the two of them follow one and the same road.

4. I go on through the things that happen according to nature, until I fall and rest. Then I shall breathe out my last breath into the air from which I draw breath every day, and fall upon the earth from which my father gathered the seed, my mother the blood, and my nurse the milk; the earth that for so many years has given me food and drink; the earth that carries me when I walk on it and misuse it in so many ways.

5. You say: "People cannot admire me for the sharpness of my wits."—Very well. But there are many other qualities of which you cannot say, "I was not made for that by nature." So show the qualities that are entirely in your power: sincerity, seriousness, endurance of hard work, turning away from pleasure, contentment with your lot and with little, kindness, frankness, no love of excess, freedom from triviality, greatness of spirit. Do you not see how many qualities you could show right now, where you have no excuse of lacking the natural gift or the aptitude? And yet you still choose to stay below the mark. Or is it because nature made you badly that you are forced to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your poor body, to try to please people, to show off, and to be so restless in your mind? No, by the gods! You could have been rid of all these things long ago. But if in truth you can be charged with being somewhat slow and dull to understand, then you must work at that too, neither neglecting it nor taking pleasure in your dullness.

6. One person, when he has done someone a kindness, is quick to put it down to that person's account as a favor owed. Another is not quick to do this, but privately he still thinks of the other as in his debt, and he knows what he has done. A third, in a sense, does not even know what he has done. He is like a vine that has produced grapes and asks for nothing more once it has borne its proper fruit. A horse that has run its race, a dog that has hunted down its prey, a bee that has made its honey: so a person who has done a good deed does not call others to come and see, but goes on to the next, as a vine goes on to bear grapes again in their season.—Must a person, then, be one of those who act this way almost without noticing it?—Yes.—But surely one must notice what one is doing. For, it may be said, it is the mark of a being made for community to be aware that he is acting for the community, and indeed to want his partner in the community to be aware of it too.—What you say is true. But you misunderstand the point now being made, and because of that you will become one of those I spoke of earlier; for they too are led astray by something that looks like reason. But if you choose to understand what that point means, do not fear that because of it you will neglect any act that serves the community.
7. A prayer of the Athenians: "Rain, rain, dear Zeus, on the plowed fields of the Athenians and on the plains." In truth, we ought either not to pray at all, or to pray in this simple and noble way.

8. When people say that Aesculapius prescribed horse-riding for this man, or cold baths, or going barefoot, we understand what they mean. In the same way we should understand it when people say that the nature of the universe prescribed for this man disease, or maiming, or loss, or anything else of the kind. In the first case "prescribed" means roughly this: he ordered it for this man as something suited to bring about his health. In the second case it means that what happens to each person has been arranged for him in a way that fits his destiny. For this is what we mean when we say that things "fit" us, just as builders say that the squared stones in walls or in pyramids "fit," when they set them together in a certain arrangement. For in all there is only one fitting together, one harmony. And just as all bodies together make the universe the body it is, so all existing causes together make necessity, or destiny, the cause it is. Even people who know nothing of all this understand what I mean, for they say: "Destiny brought this on him."—So this was brought on him, and this was prescribed for him. Let us accept these things, then, as we accept what Aesculapius prescribes. Many of his prescriptions too are unpleasant, of course, but we welcome them in the hope of health. Judge the completion and fulfillment of what the nature of the universe judges good to be the same kind of thing as your own health. So welcome everything that happens, even if it seems unpleasant, because it leads to this: to the health of the universe, and to the well-being and happiness of Zeus, that is, of the universe. For he would not have brought on anyone what he has brought, if it were not useful for the whole. Nor does the nature of anything, whatever it may be, bring about anything that does not suit what it governs. So there are two reasons why it is right to be content with what happens to you. The first is that it was done for you, was prescribed for you, and was in some way related to you, spun into your destiny from the beginning out of the most ancient causes. The second is that even what comes to each person individually contributes to the well-being and completion of the power that governs the universe, and indeed to its very continuance. For the whole is maimed if you cut off anything at all from the connection and continuity of its parts, or of its causes. And you do cut something off, as far as you are able, whenever you are discontented, and in a way try to get rid of something.

9. Do not be disgusted, or discouraged, or dissatisfied, if you do not manage to do everything according to right principles. When you have failed, go back again, and be content if most of what you do is in keeping with human nature; and love the thing you are going back to. Do not go back to philosophy as though she were a master, but as people with sore eyes go back to their bit of sponge and egg, or as someone else turns to a plaster or a dousing with water. In this way you will not fail to obey reason, and you will find rest in it. And remember that philosophy wants only what your nature wants; but you want something else, something that is not in keeping with nature.—But, it may be objected, what could be more pleasant than what I am doing?—But is this not exactly how pleasure deceives us? Consider whether greatness of spirit, freedom, simplicity, good temper and reverence for the gods are not more pleasant. And what is more pleasant than wisdom itself, when you think how secure and how smooth-running is everything that depends on the power of understanding and knowing?

10. Things are wrapped in such obscurity that quite a few philosophers, and not ordinary ones, have thought them entirely beyond understanding. Even the Stoics themselves find them hard to understand. And whatever we assent to, we may change our minds about; for where is the person who never changes? Then turn your thoughts to the things themselves, and see how short-lived and worthless they are, and how they can be owned by a filthy wretch, a prostitute or a robber. Next, turn to the characters of the people you live with: even the most agreeable of them is hard to put up with, not to mention that a person can hardly put up with himself. In such darkness and dirt, and in so constant a flow of substance and of time, of movement and of things moved, I cannot imagine what there is that deserves to be highly valued, or even seriously pursued. On the contrary, a person should comfort himself and wait for his natural breaking up, and not be irritated at the delay, but find rest in these two principles alone. The first: nothing will happen to me that is not in keeping with the nature of the universe. The second: it is in my power never to act against my god and the divine spirit within me; for there is no one who will force me to do that.

11. What am I using my soul for now? On every occasion I must ask myself this, and examine myself: What is there now in this part of me that people call the ruling faculty? And whose soul do I have now? A child's, a young man's, a weak woman's, a tyrant's, a farm animal's, or a wild beast's?

12. Even from the following we can learn what sort of things the many take to be good. If someone has first thought of certain things as truly good, such as practical wisdom, self-control, justice and courage, then once he has that idea in his mind he could not bear to hear anything said that clashed with what is truly good. But if someone has first thought of the things the many take to be good, he will listen to the comic poet's line—the one about the man so rich he has no room left to relieve himself—and gladly accept it as right on target. So even the many sense the difference. Otherwise the joke would not offend us and be rejected when applied to the first kind of good, while we accept it as apt and witty when it is said of wealth, and of the things that bring luxury and fame. Go on, then, and ask whether we should value and think good those things which, once they come to mind, invite that line of the comic poet: that their owner is so rich he has no room left to relieve himself.

13. I am made of form and matter—what shapes me and what I am made of. Neither of them will vanish into nothing, just as neither came into being out of nothing. So every part of me will be changed into some part of the universe, and that in turn will change into another part of the universe, and so on forever. It was through such a change that I too came to be, and my parents before me, and so on forever in the other direction. For nothing prevents us from saying this, even if the universe is governed in fixed cycles.

14. Reason, and the art of reasoning, are powers sufficient for themselves and for their own work. So they start from a first principle of their own and make their way to the goal set before them. That is why acts of this kind are called Catorthoseis, or right acts: the word means that they go by the right road.

15. None of those things that do not belong to a person as a human being should be called his own. They are not required of a human being; human nature does not promise them; and they are not the means by which human nature reaches its goal. So the goal of a human being does not lie in these things, nor does what helps him reach that goal—and what helps him reach it is the good. Besides, if any of these things did belong to a human being, it would not be right for him to despise them and set himself against them. Nor would someone deserve praise for showing that he does not need them; nor, if these things were really good, would someone who went without any of them be good. But as it is, the more of these things, or of others like them, a person deprives himself of, or the more patiently he bears being deprived of any of them, the better a person he is, in exactly that degree.

16. As your habitual thoughts are, so your mind will be; for the soul is dyed by its thoughts. So dye it with a steady stream of thoughts like these. For example: wherever a person can live, he can also live well. —But he must live in a palace.—Very well, then he can also live well in a palace. And again: whatever each thing was made for, that is what it was made for, and that is what it moves toward. Its goal lies in what it moves toward; and where its goal is, there too is its benefit and its good.
