Now the good of a rational being is community; for it has been shown already that we are made for community. Is it not plain that the lower exists for the sake of the higher? And living things are higher than lifeless things, and among living things the higher are those that have reason.
17. To pursue the impossible is madness; and bad people cannot help doing things of this kind.

18. Nothing happens to anyone that he is not made by nature to bear. The same things happen to someone else, and either because he does not notice that they have happened, or because he wants to show his greatness of spirit, he stands firm and comes to no harm. It is shameful, then, that ignorance and vanity should be stronger than wisdom.

19. Things themselves do not touch the soul, not in the least. They have no way into the soul, and they cannot turn or move it. The soul alone turns and moves itself; and whatever judgments it sees fit to make, it makes the things that come before it into whatever those judgments say—for itself.

20. In one respect a human being is the thing nearest to me, in so far as I must do good to people and put up with them. But in so far as some people get in the way of the actions that are mine to do, a human being becomes to me one of the things that are neither good nor bad, no less than the sun, or the wind, or a wild beast. It is true that these may hinder my action; but they do not hinder my impulses or my disposition, which can act conditionally and can change course. For the mind turns every obstacle to its activity around and makes it serve its purpose. So what hinders an action becomes a help to it; and what stands in the way on the road helps us along that road.

21. Honor what is best in the universe: that is what uses all things and directs all things. In the same way, honor what is best in yourself: it is of the same kind as what is best in the universe. For in you too, this is what uses everything else, and by this your life is directed.

22. What does no harm to the state does no harm to the citizen. Whenever something seems to have harmed you, apply this rule: if the state is not harmed by this, neither am I. But if the state is harmed, you must not be angry with the one who harmed it. Show him where he went wrong.

23. Think often of how quickly all things pass by and vanish, both the things that exist and the things that are coming into being. For substance is like a river in constant flow; the activities of things are always changing, and their causes vary endlessly; hardly anything stands still. And think of what lies close beside you: the boundless gulf of the past and of the future, into which all things vanish. How, then, is he not a fool who is puffed up over such things, or tormented by them, and makes himself miserable? They trouble him only for a time, and a short time.

24. Think of the whole of substance, of which you have a very small share; and of the whole of time, of which you have been given a short moment that cannot be divided; and of what destiny has fixed, and how small a part of it you are.

25. Does someone else do me wrong? That is his concern. He has his own disposition and his own activity. I now have what the nature of the universe wants me to have now, and I do what my own nature wants me to do now.

26. Let the ruling faculty of your soul be undisturbed by the movements in the flesh, whether of pleasure or of pain. Let it not mix itself with them, but keep within its own bounds and confine those feelings to the parts of the body where they are. But these feelings also rise up to the mind through that other sympathy, the shared feeling that naturally exists in a body which is all one. When they do, you must not try to resist the sensation, for it is natural. But the ruling faculty must not, of its own accord, add to the sensation the opinion that it is either good or bad.

27. Live with the gods. And the person who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them that his soul is content with what has been given to him, and that it does all that the divine spirit within wishes—the spirit that Zeus has given to every person as guardian and guide, a portion of himself. And this is each person's mind and reason.

28. Are you angry with someone whose armpits stink? Are you angry with someone whose breath smells? What good will your anger do you? He has that mouth, he has those armpits; such smells are bound to come from such things.—But he has reason, it will be said, and if he takes the trouble he can work out what is offensive about him.—Congratulations on your discovery! Well then, you have reason too. Use your reason to stir up his; show him his mistake, admonish him. If he listens, you will cure him, and there is no need for anger. … Neither a tragic actor nor a prostitute.

29. The way you intend to live once you have departed … you can live that way here. But if people do not let you, then leave life, yet as someone who is suffering no harm. "The house is smoky, and I am leaving it." Why do you think this is any great matter? But as long as nothing of that kind drives me out, I stay, I am free, and no one will stop me from doing what I choose; and I choose what is in keeping with the nature of a rational being made for community.

30. The intelligence that governs the universe is made for community. So it has made the lower things for the sake of the higher, and it has fitted the higher things to one another. You see how it has set some things under others and some things side by side, given each its proper share, and brought the best things together into harmony with one another.

31. How have you behaved until now toward the gods, your parents, your brothers, your children, your teachers, those who looked after you as a baby, your friends, your relatives, your slaves? Consider whether you have behaved toward all of them so far in such a way that it could be said of you: "He never wronged anyone, in deed or in word." And call to mind how much you have been through, and how much you have been able to endure; and that the story of your life is now complete and your service is over. Remember how many beautiful things you have seen, how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many so-called honors you have turned away, and how many unkind people you have treated kindly.

32. Why do unskilled and ignorant souls disturb the one who has skill and knowledge? And which soul has skill and knowledge? The one that knows the beginning and the end, and knows the reason that runs through all substance and governs the universe through all time in fixed cycles.

33. Soon, very soon, you will be ashes, or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; and a name is only a sound and an echo. The things people value most in life are empty, rotten and petty: little dogs snapping at one another, little children quarreling, laughing, and then crying the next moment. But faithfulness, modesty, justice and truth, as Hesiod says, "have fled up to Olympus from the wide earth." What is it, then, that still keeps you here, if the things the senses perceive are easily changed and never stand still, if the organs of perception are dim and easily take in false impressions, and if the poor soul itself is a vapor rising from the blood? And to be well thought of in such a world as this is an empty thing. Why, then, do you not wait calmly for your end, whether that end is extinction or a move to another place? And until that time comes, what is enough? What else but to worship the gods and praise them, to do good to people, and to practice tolerance and self-restraint? And as for everything that lies outside the limits of your poor flesh and breath, remember that it is neither yours nor in your power.

34. You can spend your life in a smooth, steady flow of happiness, if you can take the right road, and think and act in the right way. These two things are shared by the soul of God, the soul of a human being, and the soul of every rational being: first, not to be hindered by anyone else; and second, to hold that the good lies in a just disposition and in just action, and to let your desire go no further than that.
35. If this is not my own wickedness, nor the result of my own wickedness, and the common good is not harmed, why am I troubled about it? And what harm is there to the common good?

36. Do not be carried away without thinking by the way things appear. Help everyone as far as you can and as far as they deserve; and if they have suffered a loss in things that are neither good nor bad, do not imagine it to be real damage, for that is a bad habit. Instead, be like the old man who, when he left, asked for his foster child's spinning top back, knowing all the while that it was only a top. Do the same in this case too. When you are holding forth on the Rostra, the speakers' platform, have you forgotten, man, what these things really are?—Yes, but these things matter a great deal to these people.—Will you, then, be made a fool over these things too? "Once I was a fortunate man, but I lost it, I do not know how."—But being fortunate means giving yourself a good fortune; and a good fortune is a good disposition of the soul, good impulses, good actions.

chapters.title: Book 6
paragraphs: 1. The substance of the universe is obedient and yielding. The reason that governs it has nothing in itself that would cause it to do evil, because it has no malice: it does evil to nothing, and nothing is harmed by it. Everything comes into being and is brought to completion according to this reason.

2. Let it make no difference to you whether you are cold or warm, as long as you are doing your duty; whether you are drowsy or have had enough sleep; whether people speak badly of you or praise you; whether you are dying or doing something else. For dying, too, is one of the acts of life. So in this act as well, it is enough to do well the task in hand.
3. Look within. Do not let the particular quality of anything, or its worth, escape you.
4. All things that exist will soon change. Either—if indeed all substance is one—they will be turned into vapor, or they will be scattered.
5. The governing reason knows what state it is in, what it does, and what material it works on.
6. The best way to take revenge is not to become like the person who wronged you.
7. Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: moving from one act done for the common good to another, with God in mind.
8. The ruling faculty is what wakes itself up and directs itself. It makes itself whatever it is and whatever it wants to be, and it also makes everything that happens appear to it the way it wants.

9. Everything is brought about in keeping with the nature of the universe. Certainly nothing is brought about in keeping with some other nature—whether a nature that encloses this nature of the universe from outside, or one contained within it, or one that stands outside it and is independent of it.

10. The universe is either a jumble, a tangle of things that are thrown together and scattered again, or it is unity, order and providence. If it is the first, why do I want to linger in a random mixture of things, in such a mess? Why should I care about anything except how I shall one day become earth? And why am I troubled, when my elements will be scattered whatever I do? But if the second is true, then I feel reverence, I stand firm, and I trust in the one who governs.

11. When circumstances have forced you off balance in some way, come back to yourself quickly, and do not stay out of tune any longer than you are forced to be. For you will master the harmony better by returning to it again and again.

12. If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would do your duty by your stepmother, but you would still keep going back to your mother. Let the court and philosophy be your stepmother and your mother now. Go back often to philosophy and rest in her. It is through her that what you meet at court seems bearable to you, and that you seem bearable to the court.

13. When we have meat and other such food in front of us, we take in the impression that this is the dead body of a fish, and this the dead body of a bird or a pig. And again, that this Falernian wine is only a little grape juice, and this purple robe some sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shellfish. These impressions reach the things themselves and go right through them, and so we see what kind of things they really are. We ought to do the same all through life. Where things seem most worthy of our approval, we should strip them bare, look at how worthless they are, and take away all the words that make them sound grand. For outward show is a powerful twister of reason; and just when you are most sure that you are busy with things worth your trouble, that is when it deceives you most. Consider, then, what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.

14. Most of the things the crowd admires belong to the most basic kind: things held together simply by cohesion or by natural growth, such as stones, wood, fig trees, vines and olives. People who are a little more reasonable admire things held together by a principle of life, such as flocks and herds. People who are more educated still admire things held together by a rational soul. But they do not mean the soul that is rational in the universal sense. They value a soul only for being skilled in some craft or clever in some other way, or simply for owning a large number of slaves. But someone who values the rational soul—the soul that is universal and made for life as a citizen—cares about nothing else. Above all, he keeps his own soul in a condition and an activity that fit reason and life in community, and he works toward this together with those who are of the same kind as himself.

15. Some things are rushing into existence, and others are rushing out of it; and of what is coming into existence, part has already gone out. Motion and change are always renewing the world, just as the unbroken passage of time is always renewing the endless length of the ages. In this river, then, where nothing stands still, which of the things rushing past would anyone value highly? It would be like falling in love with one of the sparrows flying by—and it has already gone out of sight. The very life of each person is something like this: like the vapor given off by the blood, and the drawing in of air. For we breathe in the air once and give it back, as we do every moment; and giving back the whole power of breathing is just the same. You received that power at your birth, yesterday or the day before, and you give it back to the element from which you first drew it.

16. What is worth valuing is not giving off moisture, as plants do; nor breathing, as tame animals and wild beasts do; nor receiving impressions from the appearances of things; nor being jerked about by desires like a puppet on strings; nor gathering in herds; nor taking in food—for that is no better than separating out and getting rid of the useless part of our food. What, then, is worth valuing? Being received with clapping hands? No. Nor should we value the clapping of tongues; for the praise of the many is only a clapping of tongues. Suppose, then, that you have given up this worthless thing called fame: what is left that is worth valuing? This, I think: to move yourself and to hold yourself back in keeping with your own proper constitution—the way you are made. That is the end to which all occupations and crafts lead. For every craft aims at this: that what has been made should be fitted to the work it was made for. The vine-grower who tends the vine, the horse-breaker, and the dog-trainer all seek this end. The upbringing and teaching of the young aim at something too. Here, then, is where the value of upbringing and teaching lies. If you have this right, you will not look for anything else. Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? If not, you will be neither free, nor sufficient for your own happiness, nor free from passion. For you are bound to be envious, jealous and suspicious of those who can take those things away, and to plot against those who have what you value. Anyone who needs any of those things is bound to be in complete turmoil; and besides, he is bound to find fault with the gods again and again. But to respect and honor your own mind will make you content with yourself, in harmony with society, and in agreement with the gods—that is, praising everything they give and have ordered.

17. Above, below, all around, the elements are in motion. But the motion of virtue is not among these. It is something more divine: moving forward along a path hard to see, it goes happily on its way.

18. How strangely people behave! They will not praise those who live at the same time as they do and live alongside them; yet being praised themselves by later generations, by people they have never seen and never will see—this they value highly. But that is much the same as being upset because the people who lived before you did not praise you.

19. If something is hard for you to do, do not suppose it is impossible for a human being. But if something is possible for a human being and in keeping with human nature, believe that you can achieve it too.

20. In athletic training, suppose someone has clawed you with his nails and given you a wound by crashing into your head. Well, we do not show any sign of annoyance, we do not take offense, and we do not suspect him afterward of being treacherous. We are on our guard against him, yes—but not as an enemy, and not with suspicion; we simply keep out of his way without fuss. Let your behavior be something like this in all the other parts of life. Let us overlook a great deal in those who are like our opponents in the gymnasium. For, as I said, it is in our power to keep out of the way, and to feel neither suspicion nor hatred.

21. If anyone can convince me and show me that I am wrong in what I think or do, I will gladly change. For I am looking for the truth, and no one has ever been harmed by the truth. The one who is harmed is the person who stays in his error and ignorance.
22. I do my duty; other things do not trouble me. For those other things are either lifeless, or without reason, or things that have wandered off and do not know the way.

23. As for animals that have no reason, and things and objects in general: you have reason and they have none, so make use of them in a generous and open-handed spirit. But treat human beings, since they have reason, in a spirit of fellowship. And on every occasion call on the gods. Do not worry about how long you will go on doing this; even three hours spent this way are enough.

24. Alexander of Macedon and his stable hand were brought to the same state by death. Either they were taken back into the same generative principles of the universe, or they were both scattered alike among the atoms.

25. Consider how many things happen in each of us in the same indivisible moment—things of the body and things of the soul. Then you will not be surprised that many more things, or rather all the things that come into being, exist at the same time in the one whole that is everything, which we call the Cosmos.

26. If someone asked you how the name Antoninus is spelled, would you strain your voice and shout out each letter? And if they got angry, would you get angry too? Would you not calmly go on and name each letter in turn? In the same way, remember that in this life too every duty is made up of certain parts. Your duty is to keep to these, without being flustered and without showing anger toward those who are angry with you, and to go on your way and finish the task set before you.

27. How cruel it is not to let people strive for what seems to them suited to their nature and good for them! Yet in a way you do not let them do this when you resent their doing wrong. For they are certainly drawn toward these things because they suppose them to be suited to their nature and good for them. But what they suppose is not really so. Teach them, then, and show them, without being angry.

28. Death is an end: an end of the impressions that come through the senses, of the tugging of the strings that work our appetites, of the thoughts that run this way and that, and of service to the flesh.
29. It is shameful for the soul to give way first in this life, while your body is not giving way.

30. Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed in that dye; for it does happen. So keep yourself simple, good, pure, serious, unpretentious, a friend of justice, a worshipper of the gods, kind, affectionate, and energetic in every fitting act. Strive to remain the person philosophy wanted to make you. Revere the gods, and help people. Life is short. This earthly life has only one fruit: a reverent disposition and acts done for the common good. Do everything as a pupil of Antoninus. Remember how steady he was in every act that reason called for; how even-tempered in everything; his piety; the calm of his face; his gentleness; his disregard for empty fame; and his effort to understand things. Remember how he would never let anything pass until he had examined it very carefully and understood it clearly; how he put up with those who blamed him unjustly without blaming them in return; how he did nothing in a hurry; how he would not listen to slander; how carefully he examined people's characters and actions. He was not given to criticizing people, and he was not timid, or suspicious, or a sophist. Remember how little he was satisfied with, in lodging, bed, clothing, food and servants; how hard-working and patient he was; how, because he ate so sparingly, he could hold out until evening, not even needing to relieve himself except at the usual hour. Remember his firmness and consistency in his friendships; how he put up with people who spoke freely against his opinions; how glad he was when anyone showed him something better; and how religious he was without superstition. Imitate all this, so that when your last hour comes your conscience may be as clear as his.

31. Come back to your senses and call yourself back. Once you have woken from sleep and seen that it was only dreams that troubled you, then, now that you are awake, look at the things around you as you looked at those dreams.

32. I am made of a little body and a soul. To this little body all things are indifferent—neither good nor bad—because it cannot perceive differences. But to the understanding, only those things are indifferent that are not its own activities. Whatever things are its own activities are all in its power. And even of these, only the ones that concern the present count; for the mind's future and past activities are, for the present, indifferent too.

33. The work the hand does is not against nature, and neither is the work of the foot, as long as the foot does a foot's work and the hand a hand's. In the same way, a human being's labor is not against nature for him as a human being, as long as that labor does a human being's work. And if his labor is not against his nature, it is not bad for him either.
34. How many pleasures have been enjoyed by robbers, by men who murdered their fathers, by tyrants!

35. Do you not see how craftsmen go along up to a point with people who are not skilled in their craft, but still hold on to the principles of their art and will not bear to depart from them? Is it not strange if the architect and the doctor respect the principles of their own crafts more than a human being respects his own reason, which he shares with the gods?

36. Asia and Europe are corners of the universe; the whole sea is a drop in the universe; Mount Athos is a little clod of the universe; all of present time is a point in eternity. All things are small, changeable, perishable. All things come from there—from that ruling power of the universe—either coming directly from it or following from it as consequences. So the lion's gaping jaws, and poison, and every harmful thing, such as a thorn or mud, are by-products of what is grand and beautiful. Do not imagine, then, that they are of a different kind from what you revere; form a true judgment of the source of all things.
37. Whoever has seen the present has seen everything: all that has happened from all eternity, and all that will happen through endless time. For all things are of one kind and one form.

38. Think often about how all things in the universe are connected and related to one another. For in a way all things are woven together, and in this way they are all friendly to one another. One thing follows another in order, and this comes about through the active movement of things, the way they all breathe together as one, and the unity of their substance.
39. Fit yourself to the things that have been allotted to you; and love the people among whom you have been given your place—but love them truly, sincerely.

40. With every instrument, tool or vessel, the one who made it is not there; yet it is doing well if it does what it was made for. But in the things that nature holds together, the power that made them is inside them and stays there. So it is all the more right to revere this power, and to think that if you live and act according to its will, everything in you is in keeping with intelligence. And in the same way, in the universe too, the things that belong to it are in keeping with intelligence.

41. If you suppose that any of the things outside your power are good or bad for you, then it is inevitable that when such a bad thing happens to you, or you lose such a good thing, you will blame the gods and hate people too: those who caused the misfortune or the loss, or those you suspect of being likely to cause it. Indeed, we do much injustice because we treat these things as though they made a difference, instead of seeing them as neither good nor bad. But if we judge only what is in our power to be good or bad, there is no reason left either to find fault with God or to take a hostile stand against any human being.

42. We are all working together toward one end, some knowingly and with understanding, others without knowing what they are doing. So too are people who are asleep: it is Heraclitus, I think, who says that even they are workers and fellow workers in what happens in the universe. But people work together in different ways. Even those who find fault with what happens, and those who try to oppose it and stop it, contribute in full measure; for the universe had need even of people like these. So it remains for you to understand what kind of workers you are placing yourself among. For the one who governs all things will certainly make good use of you, and will take you in as one part among the fellow workers, those whose labors lead to one end. But do not be that kind of part—like the cheap and ridiculous line in the play that Chrysippus speaks of.

43. Does the sun take it on himself to do the work of the rain, or Aesculapius, the god of healing, the work of the Fruit-bearer, the earth? And what about each of the stars—are they not different, and yet do they not work together toward the same end?

44. If the gods have made decisions about me and about what must happen to me, they have decided well; for it is not easy even to imagine a god without forethought. And as for doing me harm, why would they have any wish to do that? What would they gain from it, or what would the whole gain—the whole that is the special object of their providence? But if they have not made decisions about me individually, they have certainly made decisions about the whole, at least; and whatever follows as a consequence of that general arrangement I ought to welcome gladly and be content with. But suppose they make decisions about nothing. It is impious to believe that; or if we do believe it, let us stop sacrificing, praying and swearing by them, and doing everything else we do as though the gods were present and living among us. But if, all the same, the gods make decisions about none of the things that concern us, then I am able to decide about myself, and I can ask what is useful. And what is useful to each person is what is in keeping with his own constitution and nature. My nature is rational and made for community. My city and country, as far as I am Antoninus, is Rome; as far as I am a human being, it is the world. So only the things that are useful to these two cities are useful to me.

45. Whatever happens to each person serves the interest of the whole. That might be enough. But if you look closely, you will also see this as a general truth: whatever is profitable to one person is profitable to other people too. But take the word "profitable" here in its everyday sense, as it is used of things in the middle—things that are neither good nor bad.

46. In the amphitheater and places like it, the constant sight of the same things, and the sameness of it all, make the show tiresome to you. It is the same with the whole of life; for everything, above and below, is the same and comes from the same things. How long, then?

47. Keep thinking of how people of every kind, of every occupation and of every nation, are dead, so that your thoughts come down even to Philistion and Phoebus and Origanion. Now turn your thoughts to the other kinds of people. To that place, then, we must go, where there are so many great orators and so many noble philosophers—Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates; so many heroes of former days, and so many generals after them, and tyrants. Besides these, there are Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes, and other people of sharp natural talent: great minds, lovers of hard work, versatile, confident, people who even mocked the perishable, short-lived life of human beings, like Menippus and others like him. Think of all these: they have long been in the dust. What harm, then, is that to them? And what harm to those whose names are not known at all? One thing here is worth a great deal: to spend your life in truth and justice, with kindness even toward liars and unjust people.

48. When you want to cheer yourself, think of the good qualities of the people who live with you: the energy of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third, some other good quality of a fourth. For nothing gives so much delight as the examples of the virtues when they show themselves in the characters of those who live with us, and appear there in as great abundance as possible. So we must keep them before our eyes.

49. You are not unhappy, I suppose, because you weigh only so many pounds and not three hundred. So do not be unhappy that you must live only so many years and not more. Just as you are satisfied with the amount of stuff you have been given to be made of, be content with your time too.

50. Let us try to persuade people. But act even against their will, when the principles of justice lead that way. If, however, someone uses force to block your way, turn to contentment and calm, and at the same time use the obstacle to practice some other virtue. And remember that you made your attempt with a reservation: you did not want to do what was impossible. What, then, did you want?—To make an attempt of just this kind.—And you achieve your aim, even if the things you set out to do are not accomplished.

51. The person who loves fame thinks his own good lies in what other people do; the person who loves pleasure thinks it lies in his own sensations; but the person who has understanding thinks his own good lies in his own actions.
52. It is in our power to hold no opinion about a thing, and not to be troubled in our soul. For things themselves have no natural power to form our judgments.
53. Train yourself to listen carefully to what someone else is saying, and as far as possible, get inside the speaker's mind.
54. What is not good for the swarm is not good for the bee either.

55. If sailors insulted the helmsman, or sick people their doctor, whom else would they listen to? Or how could the helmsman keep the people on board safe, or the doctor bring health to the people he looks after?
56. How many of those who came into the world with me have already left it.

57. To people with jaundice, honey tastes bitter; to people bitten by mad dogs, water is terrifying; and to little children, a ball is a fine thing. Why, then, am I angry? Do you think a false opinion has less power than the bile in someone with jaundice, or the poison in someone bitten by a mad dog?
58. No one will stop you from living according to the reason of your own nature; nothing will happen to you against the reason of the nature of the universe.
59. What kind of people are those whom others want to please, for what ends, and by what kinds of acts? How soon time will cover everything, and how much it has covered already.

chapters.title: Book 7
paragraphs: 1. What is badness? It is what you have often seen. And whenever anything happens, keep this in mind: it is what you have often seen. Wherever you look, high and low, you will find the same things. The old histories are full of them, and so are the histories of the times in between and of our own day; cities and houses are full of them now. There is nothing new. Everything is both familiar and short-lived.

2. How can our settled judgments die, unless the impressions—the thoughts—that go with them are put out? But it is in your power to keep fanning these thoughts into a flame. I can hold the opinion I ought to hold about anything. If I can, why am I disturbed? The things outside my mind have nothing at all to do with my mind. Let this be the state of your feelings, and you stand upright. It is in your power to get your life back. Look at things again as you used to look at them; that is what getting your life back means.

3. The empty business of putting on a show, plays on the stage, flocks of sheep, herds, drills with spears, a bone thrown to puppies, a crumb of bread tossed into a fishpond, ants toiling and carrying their loads, frightened little mice scurrying here and there, puppets jerked on strings—it is all alike. Your duty, then, in the middle of all this is to show good humor, not a haughty air. But understand, too, that each person is worth exactly as much as the things he busies himself with.

4. In conversation you must pay attention to what is being said, and in every impulse you must watch what is being done. In the one, see at once what end it is aimed at; in the other, watch carefully what is meant.

5. Is my understanding equal to this task or not? If it is, I use it for the work as a tool given to me by the nature of the universe. If it is not, then either I step back from the work and give way to someone who can do it better—unless there is some reason why I ought not to—or I do it as well as I can, taking as my helper someone who, with the support of my ruling faculty, can do what the moment calls for and what is useful for the common good. For whatever I can do, by myself or with someone else, ought to aim at one thing only: what is useful to the community and fitting for it.
6. How many who were once celebrated and famous have been handed over to oblivion; and how many of those who celebrated the fame of others are long since dead.

7. Do not be ashamed to be helped. For your task is to do your duty, like a soldier storming a city wall. What if you are lame and cannot climb onto the battlements alone, but can with someone else's help?
8. Do not let the future disturb you. You will come to it, if you have to, carrying the same reason that you now use for the present.

9. All things are woven together, and the bond between them is holy; hardly anything is unconnected with anything else. For things have been set in order together, and together they make up one and the same ordered universe. For there is one universe made up of all things, and one god who pervades all things, and one substance, and one law, one reason shared by all intelligent beings, and one truth—if indeed there is also one perfection for all beings who are of the same stock and share in the same reason.

10. Everything material soon vanishes into the substance of the whole. Everything that is form and cause is very soon taken back into the reason that governs the universe. And the memory of everything is very soon buried under time.
11. For a rational being, the same act is in keeping with nature and in keeping with reason.
12. Stand upright, or be set upright.

13. What the limbs are in a single body, rational beings are to one another, even though they exist apart; for they have been made to work together as one. You will see this more clearly if you often say to yourself: "I am a limb (melos) of the whole that rational beings make up." But if you change the l to an r and say that you are merely a part (meros), you do not yet love people from your heart. Doing good does not yet delight you for its own sake. You still do it simply because it is the proper thing to do, and not yet as a good done to yourself.

14. Let whatever chooses to fall from outside fall on the parts that can feel it. Those parts that have felt it can complain, if they like. But I am not harmed unless I judge that what has happened is bad. And it is in my power not to judge so.
15. Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good—just as if gold, or emerald, or purple dye were always saying this. Whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and keep my color.

16. The ruling faculty does not disturb itself; I mean, it does not frighten itself or bring pain on itself. If someone else can frighten it or cause it pain, let him. For it will not, by its own judgment, turn itself toward fear or pain. Let the body take care, if it can, that it suffers nothing; and if it suffers, let it say so. But the soul itself—the part that feels fear and pain, and that has full power to form an opinion about them—will suffer nothing, for it will never turn aside into judging things to be fearful or painful. The ruling faculty, in itself, needs nothing, unless it creates a need for itself. And so it is free from disturbance and free from hindrance, provided it does not disturb or hinder itself.

17. Eudaemonia—happiness—is a good divine spirit (eu, good; daemon, divine spirit), or a good thing. So what are you doing here, impression? Go away, I beg you by the gods, the way you came. I do not want you. But you have come in your old way. I am not angry with you; only go away.

18. Is anyone afraid of change? But what can come about without change? What is dearer or more fitting to the nature of the universe? Can you take a bath unless the wood that heats it is changed? Can you be fed unless your food is changed? Can anything else that is useful be done without change? Do you not see, then, that your own change is just the same, and just as necessary to the nature of the universe?

19. All bodies are carried through the substance of the universe as through a rushing torrent. By their nature they are united with the whole and work together with it, as the parts of our body work together with one another. How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has time already swallowed up! Let the same thought come to you about every person and every thing.
20. Only one thing troubles me: that I may do something the makeup of a human being does not allow, or do it in a way it does not allow, or do what it does not allow at this moment.
21. Soon you will have forgotten everything; and soon everyone will have forgotten you.

22. It is the special mark of a human being to love even those who do wrong. And this happens if, when they do wrong, it occurs to you that they are your kin; that they do wrong out of ignorance and without meaning to; that soon both of you will be dead; and above all, that the wrongdoer has done you no harm, for he has not made your ruling faculty worse than it was before.

23. The nature of the universe works the substance of the universe as if it were wax. Now it shapes a horse; then it breaks the horse up and uses the material for a tree, then for a human being, then for something else. And each of these things lasts for a very short time. But it is no hardship for any such container to be broken up, just as it was none for it to be put together.

24. A scowling face is entirely against nature. When it is put on often, all beauty dies out of the face, and at last is put out so completely that it can never be lit again. Try to conclude from this very fact that scowling is against reason. For if even the awareness of doing wrong is lost, what reason is left for living any longer?

25. The nature that governs the whole will soon change everything you see. Out of their substance it will make other things, and out of the substance of those, still others, so that the world may always be new.

26. When someone wrongs you, consider at once what opinion about good or bad led him to do it. Once you see this, you will pity him, and you will be neither surprised nor angry. For either you yourself think the same thing is good that he does, or you think something else of the same kind is good. So it is your duty to forgive him. But if you do not think such things are good or bad, you will find it easier to feel goodwill toward someone who has gone astray.

27. Do not think so much about what you do not have as about what you have. Of the things you have, pick out the best, and then consider how eagerly you would have longed for them if you did not have them. At the same time, though, be careful not to become so pleased with them that you grow used to overvaluing them, so that you would be upset if you ever lost them.
28. Withdraw into yourself. It is the nature of your rational ruling faculty to be content with itself when it acts justly, and in that way to keep its calm.

29. Wipe out the impression. Stop the jerking of the puppet strings. Keep yourself to the present. Understand clearly what is happening, whether to you or to someone else. Divide every object and sort it into what is its cause—its form—and what is its matter. Think of your last hour. Let the wrong someone has done stay where the wrong was done.
30. Pay attention to what is said. Let your mind go right into the things that are being done and into the things that do them.

31. Adorn yourself with simplicity and modesty, and with indifference toward the things that lie between virtue and vice. Love humankind. Follow God. The poet says that law rules all—and it is enough to remember that law rules all.
32. On death: whether it is a scattering, or a breaking up into atoms, or annihilation, it is either extinction or change.

33. On pain: pain that is unbearable takes us out of life; pain that lasts a long time can be borne. The mind keeps its own calm by withdrawing into itself, and the ruling faculty is not made worse. As for the parts that are harmed by the pain, let them, if they can, give their own opinion of it.

34. On fame: look at the minds of those who seek it—what they are like, what sort of things they avoid, and what sort of things they pursue. And consider this: just as heaps of sand, piled one on another, bury the sand that was there before, so in life what comes first is soon covered by what comes after.

35. From Plato: "Take a man of lofty mind, who surveys all time and all that exists. Do you suppose he can think that human life is anything great?" "It is not possible," he replied. "Then such a man will not think that death is anything bad either." "Certainly not," he said.
36. From Antisthenes: It is kingly to do good and to be badly spoken of.
37. It is shameful for the face to obey the mind, arranging and composing itself as the mind commands, while the mind is not arranged and composed by itself.
38. We should not be angry at things; for they do not care at all.
39. Give joy to the immortal gods and to us.
40. Life must be harvested like ripe ears of grain: one person is born, another dies.
41. If the gods do not care for me and my children, there is a reason for this.
42. For the good is with me, and the just.
43. No joining others in their wailing, no violent emotion.

44. From Plato: "But I would give this man a sufficient answer, and it is this: You are wrong if you think that someone who is good for anything at all should weigh up the risk of living or dying. He should rather look to this alone in everything he does: whether he is acting justly or unjustly, and doing the work of a good person or a bad one."

45. "For this is the truth of it, men of Athens: wherever someone has taken his post because he thought it the best place for him, or has been posted there by a commander, there, in my opinion, he ought to stay and face the danger. He should put nothing ahead of the shame of deserting his post—neither death nor anything else."

46. "But, my good friend, consider whether what is noble and good may be something other than saving and being saved. As for living this long or that long, at least for one who is truly a man, consider whether this may be something to put out of his thoughts. He must not be in love with life. He must leave these matters to God and believe what the women say, that no one can escape his destiny; and then the next question is how he may best live the time he has to live."
47. Watch the courses of the stars as though you were running along with them; and keep thinking about how the elements change into one another. Such thoughts wash away the filth of life on earth.

48. This is a fine saying of Plato: whoever is talking about human beings should also look at earthly things as if from some high place above them. He should look at them in their gatherings, armies, work in the fields, marriages, treaties, births, deaths, the noise of the law courts, deserted places, all the various barbarian nations, festivals, mourning, markets: a mixture of everything, and an ordered combination of opposites.

49. Look at the past—so many great changes in who holds power. From it you can foresee what is to come as well. For it will certainly have the same form; it cannot break away from the order of what happens now. So to have watched human life for forty years is the same as to have watched it for ten thousand years. For what more will you see?

50. What has grown from the earth returns to the earth; but what has sprung from heavenly seed goes back to the heavenly realms. This return is either the breaking up of the atoms' entanglement with one another, or some similar scattering of the elements, which have no feeling.
51. "With food and drink and cunning magic, turning the stream's course aside to escape from death." "The wind that heaven sends we must endure, and toil on without complaining."

52. Another person may be better at throwing his opponent in wrestling; but he is not more devoted to the common good, nor more modest, nor better trained to meet whatever happens, nor more understanding of his neighbors' faults.

53. Wherever a task can be done in keeping with the reason that gods and human beings share, there is nothing to fear. For where we can gain benefit through activity that goes well and follows the way we are made, no harm need be suspected.

54. Everywhere and always, it is in your power to accept your present situation with reverence, to deal justly with the people around you, and to work skillfully on the thoughts you have now, so that nothing slips into them without being properly examined.

55. Do not look around to find out what other people's ruling faculties are like. Look straight at this: where is nature leading you? Both the nature of the universe, through what happens to you, and your own nature, through what you must do. Every being ought to do what follows from the way it is made. And all other things have been made for the sake of rational beings—just as, among things without reason, the lower exist for the sake of the higher—but rational beings have been made for the sake of one another. The first principle in the makeup of a human being, then, is that it is made for community. The second is not to give in to the persuasions of the body. For it is the special work of rational and intelligent activity to keep within its own limits, and never to be overpowered by the stirrings of the senses or of the appetites, since both of these are animal. The activity of intelligence claims to be in charge, and does not let itself be overpowered by the stirrings of the senses and appetites. And rightly so, for nature made it to make use of all of them. The third thing in the makeup of a rational being is freedom from error and from being deceived. So let the ruling faculty hold fast to these things and go straight on its way; then it has what is its own.
56. Think of yourself as dead, as having finished your life up to this moment; and live the rest that is granted to you in keeping with nature.
57. Love only what happens to you, what is spun for you with the thread of your destiny. For what could suit you better?

58. In everything that happens, keep before your eyes those to whom the same things happened: how they resented them, treated them as strange, and found fault with them. And where are they now? Nowhere. Why, then, do you want to act the same way? Why not leave these agitations, which are foreign to nature, to those who stir them up and those who are stirred by them? Why not devote yourself entirely to making the right use of what happens to you? For then you will use it well, and it will be material for you to work on. Only pay attention to yourself, and resolve to be a good person in every act you do. And remember…
59. Look within. Within is the spring of good, and it will keep welling up, if you keep digging.

60. The body, too, should be firmly set, and show no disorder in its movement or its posture. For what the mind shows in the face, by keeping it intelligent and composed, should be required of the whole body as well. But all this should be done without putting on a show.
61. The art of living is more like the wrestler's art than the dancer's, in this respect: it should stand ready and firm to meet attacks that come suddenly and without warning.

62. Keep observing who the people are whose approval you want, and what their ruling faculties are like. For if you look at the sources of their opinions and desires, you will neither blame those who do wrong without meaning to, nor want their approval.

63. "Every soul," the philosopher says, "is deprived of truth against its will." So, in the same way, it is deprived of justice, self-control, kindness and everything of that kind against its will. It is most necessary to keep this constantly in mind, for it will make you gentler toward everyone.

64. Whenever you are in pain, have this thought ready: there is nothing shameful in it, and it does not make the mind that governs you worse. For pain does not damage that mind, either as far as it is rational or as far as it is made for community. In most pains, let this saying of Epicurus help you: pain is neither unbearable nor endless, if you remember that it has its limits and if you add nothing to it in your imagination. And remember this too: we do not notice that many things we find unpleasant are really the same as pain—such as heavy drowsiness, being scorched by heat, and having no appetite. So when you are discontented about any of these things, tell yourself that you are giving in to pain.
65. Take care that you do not feel toward inhuman people as they feel toward human beings.

66. How do we know that Telauges was not better in character than Socrates? It is not enough that Socrates died a nobler death, and argued more skillfully with the sophists, and endured a night in the cold with more toughness; that when he was ordered to arrest Leon of Salamis he thought it nobler to refuse; and that he swaggered through the streets—though one may well doubt whether that was true. What we ought to ask is what kind of soul Socrates had. Was he able to be content with being just toward people and reverent toward the gods? Was he neither pointlessly resentful of people's wickedness, nor making himself a slave to anyone's ignorance? Did he receive whatever fell to his share from the whole without treating it as strange, and without bearing it as unbearable? And did he keep his mind from sharing in the feelings of the wretched flesh?

67. Nature has not mixed the mind so closely with the body that it has left you no power to draw a boundary around yourself and keep under your own control everything that is your own. For it is very possible to be a godlike person and be recognized as such by no one. Always keep this in mind; and this too: that very little indeed is needed to live a happy life. And just because you have given up hope of becoming a skilled logician or an expert in the study of nature, do not on that account give up hope of being free and modest, made for community and obedient to God.

68. It is in your power to live free from all compulsion, in the greatest peace of mind, even if the whole world shouts against you as much as it likes, and even if wild beasts tear apart the limbs of this kneaded lump of matter that has grown around you. For in the middle of all this, what prevents the mind from keeping its calm, from judging rightly everything around it, and from being ready to use whatever is put in front of it? Then judgment can say to whatever comes before it: "This is what you really are, even if people think you look like something else." And use can say to whatever comes to hand: "You are just what I was looking for." For to me, whatever presents itself is always material for virtue, the virtue of a rational being and a citizen—in a word, material for exercising the skill that belongs to a human being or to God. For everything that happens is related either to God or to a human being; it is neither new nor hard to handle, but familiar and ready material to work on.
69. Perfection of character means this: to live each day as if it were your last, without frantic agitation, without sluggishness, and without putting on an act.

70. The gods, who are immortal, do not resent having to put up, for so long and without a break, with people such as they are, so many of them bad; and more than that, they take care of them in every way. But you, who will so soon come to an end, are you tired of putting up with the bad—and that when you are one of them yourself?
71. It is absurd for a person not to escape from his own badness, which is actually possible, but to try to escape from other people's badness, which is impossible.
72. The faculty that is rational and made for community rightly judges that whatever it finds to be neither intelligent nor made for community is beneath itself.
73. When you have done a good deed and someone else has received it, why do you still look for a third thing besides these, as fools do—to be known for having done good, or to get something back?
74. No one gets tired of receiving what is useful. And acting in keeping with nature is useful. So do not get tired of receiving what is useful by doing what is useful for others.

75. The nature of the whole set out to make the universe. But now, either everything that happens follows as a consequence of that first impulse, in an unbroken chain; or even the most important things, toward which the ruling power of the universe directs its own impulse, are governed by no rational principle. If you remember this, it will make you calmer about many things.

chapters.title: Book 8
paragraphs: 1. This thought also helps to remove the desire for empty fame: it is no longer in your power to have lived your whole life, or at least your life since youth, as a philosopher. Many others can see plainly, and so can you, that you are far from philosophy. So you have fallen into confusion, and it is no longer easy for you to win the reputation of a philosopher; and the way your life is set up works against it too. If, then, you have truly seen where the matter lies, throw away the thought of how you will look to others, and be content if you live the rest of your life in the way your nature wants. Pay attention, then, to what it wants, and let nothing else distract you. For you have wandered down many paths and found happiness nowhere—not in logical arguments, not in wealth, not in reputation, not in enjoyment, not anywhere. Where is it, then? In doing what human nature requires. And how is a person to do this? By having principles from which his impulses and his actions come. What principles? Those about good and bad: the belief that nothing is good for a human being that does not make him just, self-controlled, courageous and free; and that nothing is bad that does not do the opposite.

2. Whenever you do anything, ask yourself: How does this affect me? Will I regret it? A little while and I am dead, and everything is gone. What more do I want, if what I am doing now is the work of an intelligent living being, a being made for community, and one who lives under the same law as God?

3. Alexander and Caius and Pompeius—what are they compared with Diogenes and Heraclitus and Socrates? For these men understood things, and their causes, and the matter they are made of; and their ruling faculties were in keeping with what they pursued. But as for the others, how many things they had to worry about, and to how many things they were slaves!
4. Remember that people will go on doing the same things all the same, even if you burst with anger.

5. This is the chief thing: do not be disturbed, for everything happens according to the nature of the universe; and in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, like Hadrianus and Augustus. Next, fix your eyes steadily on the task in front of you and look at it. Remember at the same time that it is your duty to be a good person, and remember what human nature asks of you; then do that without turning aside. And speak as seems most just to you—only let it be with goodwill, with modesty, and without hypocrisy.

6. The nature of the universe has this work to do: to move what is here over there, to change things, to take them up from here and carry them there. Everything is change; yet there is no need to fear anything new. Everything is familiar to us; and the way things are shared out still remains the same.

7. Every nature is content with itself when it goes well on its way. A rational nature goes well on its way when, in its thinking, it agrees to nothing false or uncertain; when it directs its impulses only toward acts that serve the common good; when it limits its desires and aversions to the things that are in its power; and when it is satisfied with everything the common nature assigns to it. For every particular nature is a part of this common nature, as the nature of a leaf is part of the nature of the plant. The difference is that the leaf's nature is part of a nature that has no perception or reason and can be obstructed; but a human being's nature is part of a nature that cannot be obstructed, and that is intelligent and just. For that common nature gives to each thing its span of time, its substance, its cause, its activity, and what happens to it, in equal shares and according to the worth of each. But when you examine this, do not look for any one thing to be equal in every respect to any other single thing. Instead, take all the parts of one thing together and compare them with all the parts of another taken together.

8. You have no time to read. But you have time to curb arrogance; you have time to rise above pleasure and pain; you have time to rise above the love of fame, and not to be angry with stupid and ungrateful people—and even to care for them.
9. Let no one hear you complaining any longer about life at court, or about your own life.

10. Regret is a kind of self-reproach for having neglected something useful. But what is good must be something useful, and the perfectly good person should care about it. Yet no such person would ever regret having turned down a sensual pleasure. So pleasure is neither good nor useful.
11. This thing: what is it in itself, in its own makeup? What is its substance and material? What is its causal nature, or form? What is it doing in the world? And how long does it last?

12. When you are reluctant to get up from sleep, remember that doing acts that serve the community is in keeping with your own makeup and with human nature, while sleep is something we share even with animals that lack reason. And what is in keeping with each creature's own nature is also more truly its own, better suited to its nature, and indeed more pleasing too.
13. Constantly, and if possible with every impression that comes to your soul, apply to it the principles of physics (the study of nature), of ethics, and of logic.

14. Whenever you meet anyone, say to yourself at once: What opinions does this person hold about good and bad? For if he holds such and such opinions about pleasure and pain and what causes each, about fame and disgrace, about death and life, then it will not seem surprising or strange to me if he does such and such things; and I shall remember that he is compelled to act this way.

15. Remember: just as it is shameful to be surprised when a fig tree bears figs, so it is shameful to be surprised when the world produces the things it naturally produces. And it is shameful for a doctor to be surprised when someone has a fever, or for a ship's pilot to be surprised when the wind is against him.

16. Remember that changing your mind and following someone who corrects your mistake is just as much in keeping with your freedom as persisting in your mistake. For the activity is your own: it is carried out by your own impulse and your own judgment, and indeed by your own understanding too.

17. If something you find fault with is in your own power, why do you do it? And if it is in someone else's power, whom do you blame—the atoms, that is, chance, or the gods? Both are foolish. You must blame no one. If you can, correct the cause; if you cannot do that, at least correct the thing itself; and if you cannot do even that, what use is it to you to find fault? For nothing should be done without a purpose.

18. What has died does not fall out of the universe. If it stays here, it also changes here, and is broken up into its own parts, which are the elements of the universe and of yourself. And these too change, and they do not grumble.

19. Everything exists for some purpose—a horse, a vine. Why does that surprise you? Even the sun will say, "I exist for a purpose," and the rest of the gods will say the same. What, then, do you exist for? To enjoy pleasure? See whether common sense allows that.

20. In everything, nature has taken thought for the ending no less than for the beginning and the time it lasts, just like someone who throws a ball into the air. What good is it to the ball to be thrown up, or what harm to come down, or even to have fallen? And what good is it to a bubble to hold together, or what harm to burst? The same can be said of a lamp's flame too.

21. Turn the body inside out and see what sort of thing it is; and what it becomes when it grows old, and when it is diseased. Short-lived are the one who praises and the one who is praised, the one who remembers and the one who is remembered. And all this happens in a small corner of this part of the world; and even here people do not all agree with one another—no, no one even agrees with himself. And the whole earth, too, is a mere point.
22. Pay attention to what is in front of you, whether it is an opinion, an act, or a word. You deserve what you are suffering: you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.

23. Am I doing something? I do it for the good of humankind. Does something happen to me? I accept it and trace it back to the gods, and to the source of all things, from which everything that happens comes.
24. What bathing looks like to you—oil, sweat, dirt, filthy water, everything disgusting—that is what every part of life is like, and everything.

25. Lucilla saw Verus die, and then Lucilla died. Secunda saw Maximus die, and then Secunda died. Epitynchanus saw Diotimus die, and then Epitynchanus died. Antoninus saw Faustina die, and then Antoninus died. Everything is like this. Celer saw Hadrianus die, and then Celer died. And those sharp-witted men, whether seers or men puffed up with pride—where are they? Where are the sharp-witted Charax, and Demetrius the Platonist, and Eudaemon, and anyone else like them? All of them lasted only a day; all long dead. Some were not remembered even for a short time; others have become figures in legends; and others again have vanished even from the legends. Remember this, then: this little compound that is you must either be broken up, or your poor breath must be put out, or else it must be moved and placed somewhere else.

26. It brings a person satisfaction to do the proper work of a human being. And the proper work of a human being is to be kind to his own kind, to think little of the stirrings of the senses, to judge rightly the impressions that seem convincing, and to study the nature of the universe and the things that happen in it.
27. You have three relationships: one to the body that encloses you; a second to the divine cause from which everything comes to everyone; and a third to those who live alongside you.

28. Pain is either an evil to the body—in which case let the body say what it thinks of it—or to the soul. But the soul has the power to keep its own calm and peace, and not to judge that pain is an evil. For every judgment, every impulse, every desire and every aversion is within, and no evil climbs up that high.

29. Wipe out the impressions in your mind by often saying to yourself: "It is in my power now to keep this soul free of all badness, of desire, and of any disturbance at all. Rather, looking at all things, I see what their nature is, and I use each one according to its worth." Remember this power, which nature has given you.
30. Speak in the senate and to every person, whoever he may be, fittingly and without putting on airs. Use plain speech.

31. Augustus's court: his wife, his daughter, his descendants, his ancestors, his sister, Agrippa, his relatives, his close companions, his friends; Areius, Maecenas, his doctors and his sacrificing priests—the whole court is dead. Then turn to the others. Consider not the death of a single person but the death of a whole family, such as the family of the Pompeii; and consider the words inscribed on tombs: "The last of his line." Then think how hard the people before them worked to leave an heir; and then that, of necessity, someone has to be the last. Here again, consider the death of a whole family line.

32. It is your duty to put your life in good order one act at a time; and if each act does its duty as far as possible, be content. No one can stop you from making each act do its duty. "But something from outside will stand in the way." Nothing will stand in the way of your acting justly, with self-control, and with good sense. "But perhaps some other kind of activity will be hindered." Well, if you accept the hindrance calmly and are content to turn your efforts to what is allowed, another opportunity for action is at once put before you in place of the one that was hindered. And it is one that will fit into the ordering of life we are speaking of.
33. Receive wealth or prosperity without arrogance; and be ready to let it go.

34. If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a head, lying somewhere apart from the rest of the body—that is what a person makes of himself, as far as he can, when he is not content with what happens, and cuts himself off from others, or does anything that sets him against others. Suppose you have broken away from the natural unity—for you were made by nature as a part, but now you have cut yourself off. Still, here is a beautiful provision: it is in your power to join yourself to it again. God has allowed no other part to come back together once it has been separated and cut away. But consider the kindness with which he has honored human beings: he has put it in their power not to be separated from the whole at all; and when they have been separated, he has allowed them to return, to be united with it again, and to take up their place as a part once more.

35. Just as the nature of the universe has given each rational being all the other powers it has, so we have also received from it the following power. The nature of the universe takes everything that stands in its way and opposes it: it turns that obstacle around, fixes it in its destined place, and makes it part of itself. In the same way, a rational being is able to make every obstacle into material for itself, and to use it for whatever purpose it may have set out to achieve.

36. Do not upset yourself by picturing your whole life at once. Do not let your thoughts take in, all together, all the various troubles you may expect to happen to you. Instead, each time one comes, ask yourself: What is there in this that is unbearable and beyond enduring? You will be ashamed to admit it. Next, remember that it is neither the future nor the past that weighs on you, but only the present. And the present shrinks to very little if you only mark off its limits, and if you scold your mind when it cannot hold out against even this much.

37. Do Panthea or Pergamus sit by the tomb of Verus now? Does Chaurias or Diotimus sit by the tomb of Hadrianus? That would be ridiculous. Well, suppose they did sit there: would the dead know it? And if the dead knew it, would they be pleased? And if they were pleased, would that make them immortal? Was it not fated that these mourners too would first become old women and old men, and then die? And once these mourners were dead, what would the dead do then? All this is foul smell and blood in a bag.
38. "If you can see sharply, look and judge wisely," says the philosopher.
39. In the makeup of a rational being I see no virtue that stands opposed to justice; but I do see a virtue that stands opposed to the love of pleasure, and that is self-control.

40. If you take away your opinion about whatever seems to be causing you pain, you yourself stand completely safe. "Who is this 'yourself'?" "Reason." "But I am not reason." "So be it. Then let reason itself not trouble itself. And if some other part of you is suffering, let that part form its own opinion about itself."

41. Whatever hinders perception by the senses is bad for an animal's nature. Whatever hinders its impulses—its desires—is equally bad for an animal's nature. And in the same way, something else hinders plants and is bad for their makeup. So, then, whatever hinders the intelligence is bad for an intelligent nature. Apply all this to yourself, then. Does pain or physical pleasure lay hold of you? That is for the senses to look to. Has some obstacle blocked you while you were striving toward something? If you were striving for it unconditionally, without any reservation, then this obstacle really is bad for you as a rational being. But if you took into account how things usually go, you have not yet been harmed, or even hindered. As for the things that belong properly to the understanding, no one else is in the habit of hindering them; for neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant, nor insults can touch the understanding in any way. Once the understanding has become a sphere, it stays a sphere.
42. It is not right for me to cause myself pain, for I have never deliberately caused pain even to anyone else.

43. Different things delight different people; my delight is to keep my ruling faculty sound: not turning away from any person, or from anything that happens to people, but looking at everything and receiving it all with welcoming eyes, and using each thing according to its worth.

44. Make sure you take hold of this present time for yourself. For those who would rather chase fame after death do not stop to think that the people of later times will be just like these people they cannot stand now; and both are mortal. And what is it to you, in any way, if these later people utter this or that sound, or hold this or that opinion about you?

45. Take me and throw me wherever you like. For there I shall keep the divine spirit within me calm—that is, content—so long as it can feel and act in keeping with its own proper makeup. Is this change of place reason enough for my soul to be unhappy and worse off than before—cast down, swelling up, shrinking back, frightened? And what will you find that is reason enough for that?

46. Nothing can happen to any human being that is not the kind of thing that happens to human beings; nothing to an ox that is not in keeping with the nature of an ox; nothing to a vine that is not in keeping with the nature of a vine; nothing to a stone that is not proper to a stone. If, then, what happens to each thing is both usual and natural, why should you complain? For the common nature brings you nothing that you cannot bear.

47. If you are pained by something outside you, it is not that thing that troubles you, but your own judgment about it. And it is in your power to wipe that judgment out right now. But if something in your own character pains you, who is stopping you from correcting your opinion? And even if you are pained because you are not doing some particular thing that seems right to you, why not act instead of complaining? "But what if some obstacle too strong for me is in the way?" Then do not be grieved, for the reason it is not being done does not depend on you. "But life is not worth living if this cannot be done." Then leave life contentedly, just as someone dies who is still in the midst of his work—and leave it well pleased, too, with the things that stand in your way.

48. Remember that the ruling faculty cannot be conquered when it gathers itself together and is satisfied with itself, as long as it does nothing it does not choose to do, even when its resistance is mere stubbornness. What, then, will it be like when it judges something with the help of reason and after careful thought? That is why a mind free from passions is a fortress: a human being has nothing more secure to run to for refuge, where from then on he cannot be captured. Whoever has not seen this is ignorant; but whoever has seen it and does not run to this refuge is unhappy.

49. Tell yourself nothing beyond what your impressions report at first sight. Suppose you have been told that someone is speaking badly of you. That much has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported. I see that my child is sick. That I do see; but that he is in danger, I do not see. So always keep to what appears at first sight, and add nothing to it yourself from within; then nothing happens to you. Or rather, do add something—but add it as someone familiar with everything that happens in the world.

50. A cucumber is bitter: throw it away. There are briars in the road: step aside from them. That is enough. Do not go on to add, "And why were such things made in the world?" For someone who understands nature would laugh at you, just as a carpenter and a shoemaker would laugh at you if you found fault because you saw in their workshop the shavings and scraps from the things they make. And yet they have places where they can throw away those shavings and scraps, while the nature of the universe has no space outside itself. The wonderful thing about nature's art is that, although she has set limits around herself, she takes everything within her that seems to be decaying, growing old and useless, changes it into herself, and makes new things again out of these very same materials. So she needs no material from outside, and no place into which to throw what decays. She is content, then, with her own space, her own matter, and her own art.

51. Do not be sluggish in what you do, or muddled in what you say, or wandering in your thoughts. Do not let your soul be at war with itself within, or spill out of itself. And do not be so busy in life that you have no leisure. Suppose people kill you, cut you to pieces, curse you. How can any of this stop your mind from staying pure, wise, sober and just? It is as if someone stood beside a clear, pure spring and cursed it: the spring never stops sending up drinkable water. And if he throws mud or filth into it, it will quickly scatter them and wash them out, and will not be polluted at all. How, then, will you have a spring that never runs dry, and not a mere well? By shaping yourself, every hour, toward freedom—together with contentment, simplicity and modesty.

52. Whoever does not know what the world is does not know where he is. And whoever does not know what the world exists for does not know who he is, or what the world is. And whoever has failed to know any one of these things could not even say what he himself exists for. What, then, do you think of someone who avoids or seeks the praise of people who applaud—people who know neither where they are nor who they are?

53. Do you want to be praised by someone who curses himself three times an hour? Do you want to please someone who does not please himself? Does anyone please himself who regrets nearly everything he does?

54. Do not let your breathing any longer be the only thing in tune with the air around you; let your intelligence now also be in harmony with the intelligence that embraces all things. For that intelligent power is spread through every part and runs through all things for anyone willing to draw it in, no less than the power of the air is there for anyone able to breathe it.

55. In general, wickedness does no harm at all to the universe; and in particular, one person's wickedness does no harm to another. It harms only the one person who has the power to be free of it as soon as he chooses.

56. To my own free will, my neighbor's free will is just as indifferent—neither good nor bad for it—as his poor breath and flesh are. For even though we are made above all for the sake of one another, still the ruling faculty of each of us has its own proper work. Otherwise my neighbor's wickedness would be my harm; and God has not willed this, because he did not want my unhappiness to depend on someone else.

57. The sun seems to be poured down, and it does indeed spread out in every direction, yet it is not poured away. For this spreading is a stretching out. That is why its rays are called aktines, "extensions": in Greek the name comes from their being stretched out, apo tou ekteinesthai. You can judge what kind of thing a ray is if you watch sunlight coming through a narrow opening into a darkened room. It stretches out in a straight line, and it is, as it were, broken off when it meets some solid body that stands in its way and cuts off the air beyond. But there the light stays fixed; it does not slide off or fall away. This, then, is how the understanding should pour itself out and spread: never pouring away, but stretching out. It should not crash violently or headlong into the obstacles in its way; nor should it fall down, but stay fixed and light up whatever receives it. For a body that does not let the light in deprives itself of the light.

58. Whoever fears death fears either losing all sensation or having a different kind of sensation. But if you have no sensation, you will not feel any harm either; and if you gain another kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living being, and you will not stop living.
