59. Human beings exist for the sake of one another. So teach them, or bear with them.
60. An arrow moves in one way, the mind in another. Yet the mind, both when it is being cautious and when it is busy examining something, moves straight ahead all the same, toward its target.
61. Enter into every person's ruling faculty; and let every other person enter into yours as well.

chapters.title: Book 9
paragraphs: 1. Whoever acts unjustly acts impiously. For the nature of the universe has made rational beings for the sake of one another: to help one another as each deserves, and never to harm one another. So whoever goes against her will is plainly guilty of impiety toward the highest divinity. Whoever lies is also guilty of impiety toward the same divinity. For the nature of the universe is the nature of the things that exist, and the things that exist are bound up with everything that comes into being. Further, this nature of the universe is called truth, and it is the first cause of everything that is true. So whoever lies on purpose is guilty of impiety, because by deceiving he acts unjustly. And whoever lies without meaning to is guilty too, because he is at odds with the nature of the universe, and because he disturbs its order by fighting against the nature of the world. For anyone who is carried, of his own accord, toward what is contrary to truth is fighting against it. For nature had given him the powers to tell falsehood from truth, and because he neglected them he can no longer do so. And whoever pursues pleasure as good and avoids pain as bad is guilty of impiety as well. For such a person is bound to find fault with the nature of the universe again and again. He will complain that it hands out things to bad people and good people contrary to what they deserve, because bad people often enjoy pleasure and own the things that bring it, while good people get pain as their share, and the things that cause pain. Further, whoever is afraid of pain will sometimes be afraid of some of the things that are going to happen in the world, and that in itself is impiety. And whoever pursues pleasure will not keep away from injustice, and that is plainly impiety. Now there are pairs of things toward which the nature of the universe is equally disposed; for it would not have made both things in each pair unless it were equally disposed toward both. Those who want to follow nature should be of one mind with it about these things, and equally disposed toward them too. Pain and pleasure, death and life, honor and dishonor: the nature of the universe makes use of these equally. So whoever is not equally disposed toward them is plainly acting impiously. When I say that the nature of the universe makes use of them equally, I mean that they happen alike to the things that come into being one after another in a continuous chain, and to the things that come after them. They happen by virtue of a certain original impulse of providence. By that impulse providence moved, from a certain beginning, to the present ordering of things. Providence conceived certain principles of all that was to be, and it fixed the powers that would produce beings, and changes, and successions of that kind.

2. The happiest lot for a person would be to leave humankind without ever having tasted lying or hypocrisy or luxury or pride. The next best voyage, as the saying goes, is to breathe out your life once you have had your fill of these things. Have you decided to stay on with vice? Has experience still not persuaded you to flee from this plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague—far more so than any such foulness and change in the air that surrounds us. The foulness of the air is a plague to animals insofar as they are animals; but the corruption of the mind is a plague to human beings insofar as they are human.

3. Do not despise death; be well content with it, since this too is one of the things nature wills. Think of being young and growing old, growing up and reaching full strength, getting teeth and a beard and gray hair, begetting, being pregnant and giving birth, and all the other natural processes that the seasons of your life bring: dissolution is just like these. So this is the attitude of a thoughtful person toward death: not careless, not impatient, not contemptuous, but waiting for it as one of the processes of nature. Just as you now wait for the time when the child will come out of your wife's womb, so be ready for the time when your soul will fall out of this casing. But if you also want a plain, ordinary comfort that will reach your heart, nothing will reconcile you to death better than looking at the things you are about to be taken away from, and at the character of the people with whom your soul will no longer be mingled. Not that it is in any way right to take offense at them; it is your duty to care for them and to bear with them gently. Yet remember that you will not be leaving people who share your principles. For this is the only thing, if there is anything, that could pull us the other way and hold us to life: to be allowed to live with people who share our principles. But as it is, you see how wearing it is when those who live together are out of tune with one another—so much that you might say: Come quickly, death, in case I too should forget myself.
4. Whoever does wrong does wrong to himself. Whoever acts unjustly acts unjustly toward himself, because he makes himself bad.
5. Often a person acts unjustly by not doing something, not only by doing something.
6. Your present judgment, grounded in understanding; your present action, aimed at the common good; your present state of mind, content with everything that happens—that is enough.
7. Wipe out the impression. Check desire. Quench appetite. Keep the ruling faculty in its own control.

8. Among the animals that have no reason, one life is shared out; among rational beings, one intelligent soul is shared out. In the same way there is one earth for all things made of earth, and all of us who have sight, and all of us who have life, see by one light and breathe one air.

9. All things that share in something common to them all move toward what is of their own kind. Everything made of earth tends toward the earth. Everything liquid flows together. Everything of the nature of air does the same, so that something is needed to keep them apart, and force has to be applied. Fire does move upward, drawn by the elemental fire above; but it is so ready to catch and burn together with all the fire here below that any material that is at all dry is easily set alight, because less of what hinders burning is mixed into it. In the same way, then, everything that shares in the common intelligent nature moves just as much toward what is of its own kind—or even more. For the higher it stands above all other things, the readier it is to mingle and merge with what is akin to it. So among animals without reason we find swarms of bees, herds of cattle, birds rearing their young, and something like love. For even animals have souls, and the power that draws them together is seen working in them more strongly, in a way never observed in plants or stones or trees. Among rational beings there are political communities and friendships, families and gatherings; and in wars, treaties and truces. And among things higher still, even though they are far apart from one another, a kind of unity exists, as in the stars. So rising to a higher level can produce a fellow-feeling even between things that are separated. See, then, what happens now. Only intelligent beings have now forgotten this desire and inclination for one another; in them alone this flowing together is not seen. And yet, though people try to escape this union, they are caught and held by it, for their nature is too strong for them. You will see what I mean if you only watch. So you would sooner find something made of earth that touches nothing earthy than a human being cut off entirely from other human beings.

10. A human being bears fruit, and so do God and the universe; each bears it in its proper season. And if ordinary usage applies the phrase 'bearing fruit' especially to the vine and the like, that does not matter. Reason bears fruit both for everyone and for itself, and from it come other things of the same kind as reason itself.

11. If you can, set those who do wrong right by teaching them. If you cannot, remember that kindness was given to you for this very purpose. The gods too are kind to such people; for some purposes they even help them to health, wealth and reputation—that is how kind they are. You too have it in your power to be like this; or tell me, who is stopping you?

12. Do not work like someone who is wretched, nor like someone who wants to be pitied or admired. Direct your will to one thing only: to set yourself moving and to hold yourself back, as reason, made for community, requires.
13. Today I got out of all trouble—or rather, I threw all trouble out. For it was not outside me; it was inside, in my opinions.
14. All things are the same: familiar from experience, lasting only a day, worthless in what they are made of. Everything now is just as it was in the days of those we have buried.
15. Things stand outside us, just themselves, by themselves. They know nothing about themselves, and they pass no judgment. What is it, then, that judges them? The ruling faculty.
16. The good and the bad of a rational being made for community lie not in what he undergoes but in what he does—just as his virtue and his vice lie not in what he undergoes but in what he does.
17. For a stone thrown into the air, it is nothing bad to come down, and nothing good to have been carried up.
18. Look deep into people's ruling faculties, and you will see what judges you are afraid of, and what sort of judges they are when they judge themselves.
19. Everything is changing. You yourself are constantly changing, and in a way constantly being destroyed; and so is the whole universe.
20. You must leave another person's wrongdoing where it is.

21. When activity ends, when impulse and opinion come to a stop—in a sense, when they die—that is nothing bad. Now think about your life: your life as a child, as a youth, as a grown man, as an old man. In these too every change was a death. Is this anything to fear? Now think about your life under your grandfather, then under your mother, then under your father. And as you find many other differences and changes and endings, ask yourself: Is this anything to fear? In the same way, then, the ending and stopping and changing of your whole life is nothing to fear either.

22. Hurry to examine your own ruling faculty, and the ruling faculty of the universe, and your neighbor's. Your own, so that you can make it just. The universe's, so that you remember what you are a part of. Your neighbor's, so that you know whether he acted in ignorance or with knowledge, and so that you also bear in mind that his ruling faculty is akin to yours.

23. Just as you yourself are one of the parts that make up a community, so let every act of yours be one of the parts that make up the life of the community. So any act of yours that has no bearing, direct or distant, on the common good tears your life apart and does not let it be one whole. It is a kind of mutiny—like a man in a public assembly who goes his own way and stands apart from the general agreement.

24. Children's quarrels and their games, and poor little souls carrying corpses around—that is what everything is. And so what is shown in the scene of the dwellings of the dead strikes our eyes all the more clearly.

25. Look closely at what kind of form a thing has. Separate it completely from its material, and consider it by itself. Then work out the longest time that a thing of that particular form is naturally made to last.
26. You have put up with endless troubles because you were not content with your ruling faculty doing what nature made it to do. But enough of this.

27. When someone blames you or hates you, or when people say something hurtful about you, go up to their poor souls, get inside them, and see what sort of people they are. You will find that there is no reason to trouble yourself about whether these people hold this or that opinion of you. Still, you must wish them well, for by nature they are friends. And the gods too help them in every way, by dreams and by signs, to get the things they care about.

28. The cycles of the universe are always the same, up and down, from age to age. Either the intelligence of the universe sets itself in motion for each separate thing that happens—and if so, be content with what its activity brings about. Or it sets itself in motion once, and everything else follows from that, in a way, as a consequence. Or indivisible elements are the origin of all things. In a word: if there is a god, all is well; and if chance rules, do not let yourself be ruled by chance too. Soon the earth will cover us all. Then the earth too will change, and the things that come out of that change will go on changing forever, and those in turn forever. For anyone who reflects on these changes and transformations, following one another like wave after wave, and on how fast they come, will look down on everything that perishes.

29. The cause of the universe is like a winter torrent: it sweeps everything along. How worthless they are, these poor little men who busy themselves with public affairs and imagine they are acting as philosophers! Drivelling fools, all of them. Well then, man, do what nature asks of you now. Get moving, if it is in your power, and do not look around to see whether anyone will notice. Do not hope for Plato's Republic; be content if the smallest thing goes forward well, and consider that result no small matter. For who can change people's opinions? And without a change of opinions, what is there but the slavery of people who groan while they pretend to obey? Come now, tell me about Alexander and Philippus and Demetrius of Phalerum. They themselves will judge whether they understood what the common nature required and trained themselves accordingly. But if they acted like heroes in a tragedy, no one has condemned me to imitate them. The work of philosophy is simple and modest. Do not lead me astray into arrogance and pride.

30. Look down from above on the countless herds of human beings, their countless ceremonies, their endlessly varied voyages in storm and calm, and the differences among those who are born, who live together, and who die. Consider too the life that others lived long ago, and the life of those who will live after you, and the life lived now among foreign peoples. Consider how many do not even know your name, and how many will soon forget it, and how those who are perhaps praising you now will very soon be blaming you. And consider that neither a name after death is worth anything, nor reputation, nor anything else.

31. Toward what comes from the cause outside you, let there be freedom from disturbance. In what you do from the cause within you, let there be justice. That is, let your impulse and your action end in this—in acts that serve the community; for this is in keeping with your nature.

32. You can clear out of your way many of the useless things that disturb you, for they exist entirely in your opinion. And then you will make plenty of room for yourself: by taking in the whole universe with your mind, by contemplating the eternity of time, and by observing how quickly each separate thing changes—how short the time is from birth to dissolution, how boundless the time before birth, and how equally endless the time after dissolution!

33. Everything you see will soon perish, and those who watched it perish will very soon perish too. And the one who dies in extreme old age will end up in the same state as the one who died before his time.

34. What are these people's ruling faculties like? What sort of things are they busy with? For what sort of reasons do they love and honor? Picture their poor souls laid bare. When they think their blame does harm or their praise does good—what an idea!

35. Loss is nothing but change. And the nature of the universe delights in change. In obedience to her, all things are done well now; they have been of the same form from eternity, and they will be so through endless time. What, then, are you saying? That all things have been bad and always will be bad? That among so many gods no power has ever been found to set these things right, and the world has been condemned to be bound in evils that never end?

36. The rottenness of the matter that underlies everything! Water, dust, bones, filth. Or again: marble, the calluses of the earth; gold and silver, its sediments; clothes, just bits of hair; purple dye, blood; and everything else is of the same kind. And the breath that is part of us is also another thing of the same kind, changing from this into that.

37. Enough of this wretched life, this grumbling, these monkey tricks! Why are you disturbed? What is new in this? What is unsettling you? Is it the form of the thing? Look at it. Or is it the matter? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing. So toward the gods, now at last, become simpler and better. It is all the same whether we study these things for a hundred years or for three.
38. If someone has done wrong, the harm is his own. But perhaps he has not done wrong.

39. Either all things come from one intelligent source and come together as in one body—and then the part ought not to find fault with what is done for the good of the whole. Or there are only atoms, and nothing but mixing and scattering. So why are you disturbed? Say to your ruling faculty: Are you dead? Are you corrupted? Are you playing the hypocrite? Have you become a beast? Do you herd and graze with the rest?

40. Either the gods have no power, or they have power. If they have no power, why do you pray to them? But if they do have power, why not pray for them to give you the ability not to fear any of the things you fear, or not to desire any of the things you desire, or not to be pained by anything—rather than praying that this or that should not happen, or should happen? For surely, if they can help human beings at all, they can help them with this. But perhaps you will say that the gods have put these things in your power. Well then, is it not better to use what is in your power like a free person than to long, like a cringing slave, for what is not in your power? And who told you that the gods do not help us even with the things that are in our power? Start praying for such things, then, and you will see. One man prays: How can I sleep with that woman? You pray: How can I stop wanting to sleep with her? Another prays: How can I be rid of this? You pray: How can I stop wanting to be rid of it? Another: How can I keep from losing my little son? You: How can I stop being afraid of losing him? In short, turn your prayers this way, and see what happens.

41. Epicurus says: In my illness I did not talk about my bodily sufferings; nor, he says, did I discuss such things with those who came to see me. I went on discussing the nature of things as before, keeping to this main point: how the mind, while it shares in the movements that go on in the poor flesh, can stay free from disturbance and keep hold of its own proper good. Nor did I, he says, give the doctors a chance to put on solemn faces as if they were doing something important; my life went on well and happily. So do what he did, in sickness if you are sick, and in any other situation. For it is a principle of every school of philosophy never to abandon philosophy, whatever happens to us, and never to chatter idly with an ignorant person or with someone who knows nothing of nature, but to be intent only on what you are doing now, and on the instrument you are doing it with.

42. When someone's shameless behavior offends you, ask yourself at once: Is it possible, then, for there to be no shameless people in the world? It is not possible. So do not ask for the impossible. This person too is one of the shameless people who must necessarily exist in the world. Keep the same thought ready for the scoundrel, the untrustworthy person, and anyone who does wrong in any way. For as soon as you remind yourself that it is impossible for such people not to exist, you will become kinder toward each of them individually. It is useful, too, to think at once, as the occasion arises, what virtue nature has given human beings to set against each wrong act. For she has given us gentleness as an antidote to the stupid person, and against another kind of person some other power. And in every case you can set right, by teaching, the person who has gone astray; for everyone who does wrong misses his aim and has gone astray. Besides, how have you been harmed? You will find that none of the people you are irritated with has done anything that could make your mind worse; and what is bad and harmful for you exists only in the mind. What harm is done, or what is strange, if an untaught person acts like an untaught person? Consider whether you should not rather blame yourself, for not expecting that such a person would go wrong in this way. Your reason gave you the means to suppose that he was likely to make this mistake; yet you forgot, and now you are amazed that he has made it. But above all, when you blame someone as untrustworthy or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For the fault is plainly your own: either you trusted that a person of such a character would keep his promise, or, when you did him a kindness, you did not do it unconditionally, nor in such a way that you took all your profit from the act itself. For what more do you want when you have done someone a good turn? Are you not content to have done something in keeping with your nature? Do you want to be paid for it? That is as if the eye demanded a reward for seeing, or the feet for walking. For these parts of the body are made for a particular purpose, and by working according to their own makeup they receive what is their own. In the same way, a human being is made by nature to do good to others; so when he has done something kind, or anything else that serves the common good, he has acted according to his own makeup, and he has what is his own.

chapters.title: Book 10
paragraphs: 1. Will you never, then, my soul, be good and simple, unified and naked, plainer to see than the body that surrounds you? Will you never know what it is to have an affectionate and contented disposition? Will you never be full, lacking nothing, longing for nothing more, wanting nothing, no living thing and no lifeless thing, for the sake of enjoying pleasures? Will you never stop wanting more time in which to enjoy them longer, or a place, or a pleasant climate, or people you could live with in harmony? Will you not instead be satisfied with your present condition and pleased with everything around you? Will you not convince yourself that you have everything, and that it comes from the gods; that everything is well with you, and will be well, whatever pleases the gods and whatever they will give for the preservation of the perfect living being, the universe? That being is good and just and beautiful. It brings all things into being and holds them together, and it contains and embraces all the things that are broken up so that other things like them can be produced. Will you never be the kind of person who lives in community with gods and human beings in such a way that you never find fault with them at all, and they never condemn you?

2. Observe what your nature requires insofar as you are governed by nature alone. Then do it and accept it, provided that your nature as a living creature will not be made worse by it. Next you must observe what your nature requires insofar as you are a living creature. And you may allow yourself all of this, provided that your nature as a rational being will not be made worse by it. And a rational being is, by that very fact, also a political being, made for community. Follow these rules, then, and do not trouble yourself about anything else.

3. Everything that happens either happens in a way that nature has formed you to bear, or in a way that nature has not formed you to bear. If it happens to you in a way nature has formed you to bear, do not complain; bear it as nature formed you to bear it. But if it happens in a way nature has not formed you to bear, do not complain either; for once what happens has consumed you, it will perish. Remember, however, that nature has formed you to bear everything that your own opinion can make bearable and tolerable, by thinking that bearing it is either in your interest or your duty.
4. If someone is mistaken, teach him kindly and show him his error. But if you cannot, blame yourself, or not even yourself.
5. Whatever happens to you was prepared for you from all eternity. From eternity, the interwoven chain of causes was spinning together the thread of your existence and of everything that befalls it.

6. Whether the universe is a collection of atoms, or nature is a system, let this be settled first: I am a part of the whole, which is governed by nature. Second, I am in some way closely related to the other parts that are of the same kind as myself. If I remember this, then, since I am a part, I shall not be discontented with anything that is assigned to me from the whole. For nothing is harmful to the part if it is to the benefit of the whole. The whole contains nothing that is not to its own benefit, and all natures, indeed, have this principle in common; but the nature of the universe has this further principle: it cannot be forced, even by any cause outside itself, to produce anything harmful to itself. So by remembering that I am a part of such a whole, I shall be content with everything that happens. And since I am in some way closely related to the parts that are of the same kind as myself, I shall do nothing that sets me against others. Instead I shall turn toward those who are of the same kind as myself; I shall direct all my efforts to the common good and turn them away from what is contrary to it. Now if things are done in this way, life must flow on happily, just as you can see that a citizen's life is happy when he keeps to a course of action that benefits his fellow citizens and is content with whatever the state assigns to him.

7. The parts of the whole, by which I mean everything that is naturally contained in the universe, must of necessity perish. But understand "perish" in this sense: they must undergo change. Now if this change were by nature both an evil and a necessity for the parts, the whole would not continue in good condition, since its parts are subject to change and are made to perish in various ways. For did Nature herself set out to do evil to the things that are parts of herself, to make them subject to evil and bound by necessity to fall into it? Or did such results come about without her knowing? Both suppositions are incredible. But suppose someone even drops the word Nature, as a power that makes things, and speaks of these things simply as natural. Even then it would be ridiculous to say, on the one hand, that the parts of the whole are by their nature subject to change, and on the other hand to be surprised or resentful as if something were happening against nature. This is especially so since things break up into the very things each of them is made of. For either the elements out of which everything was put together are scattered, or there is a change: what is solid turns to earth, and what is airy turns to air. In this way these parts are taken back into the reason that governs the universe, whether the universe is consumed by fire at fixed periods or renewed by everlasting changes. And do not imagine that the solid part and the airy part have belonged to you since your birth. All of this came into you only yesterday or the day before, so to speak, from the food you ate and the air you breathed in. So what changes is this part that came in, not what your mother gave birth to. And suppose that what your mother gave birth to does bind you very closely to that other part, the incoming one with its own quality of change. Even so, this is no objection at all to what has been said.

8. When you have taken on these names, good, modest, truthful, rational, a person of equanimity, a person of greatness of soul, take care that you do not exchange them for others; and if you should lose them, return to them quickly. And remember that "rational" was meant to signify careful, discerning attention to each individual thing, and freedom from carelessness. "Equanimity" means willingly accepting the things that the common nature assigns to you. "Greatness of soul" means lifting the thinking part of you above the pleasant or painful sensations of the flesh, above that poor thing called fame, above death, and above everything of that kind. If, then, you keep hold of these names, without wanting others to call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life. For to go on being what you have been until now, and to be torn to pieces and soiled in such a life, is the mark of someone very stupid and too fond of his life. He is like those half-eaten fighters in the arena with wild beasts who, though covered with wounds and blood, still beg to be kept alive until the next day, when they will be thrown, in the same state, to the same claws and the same bites. So make yourself secure in these few names. If you are able to stay in them, stay there, as if you had been carried off to some Islands of the Blessed. But if you notice that you are falling out of them and are not keeping your hold, go bravely into some corner where you will keep hold of them; or else leave life at once, not in passion, but simply, freely and modestly, having done at least this one good thing in your life: that you left it in this way. It will greatly help you to remember these names, however, if you remember the gods: that they do not want to be flattered, but want all rational beings to be made like themselves. And remember that what does the work of a fig tree is a fig tree, that what does the work of a dog is a dog, that what does the work of a bee is a bee, and that what does the work of a human being is a human being.

9. Farce, war, panic, sluggishness, slavery: day by day these will wipe out those sacred principles of yours. How many things do you form impressions of without any study of nature? And how many do you neglect? But you ought to look at everything and do everything in such a way that, at one and the same time, your power of dealing with circumstances is perfected, your power of contemplation is exercised, and the confidence that comes from knowing each individual thing is kept up, not shown off, and yet not hidden either. For when will you enjoy simplicity? When will you enjoy seriousness? And when will you enjoy knowing each individual thing: what it is in its substance, what place it has in the universe, how long it is formed to last, what things it is made of, to whom it can belong, and who are able both to give it and to take it away?

10. A spider is proud when it has caught a fly; one man is proud when he has caught a poor hare, another when he has caught a little fish in a net, another when he has caught wild boars, another bears, another Sarmatians. If you examine their judgments, are they not all robbers?

11. Acquire the contemplative way of seeing how all things change into one another. Attend to it constantly, and train yourself in this part of philosophy. For nothing is so well suited to produce greatness of soul. A person of such greatness of soul has stripped off the body. He sees that he must, no one knows how soon, leave the company of human beings and leave everything here; and so he gives himself wholly to acting justly in everything he does, and in everything else that happens he gives himself over to the nature of the universe. As for what anyone will say or think about him, or do against him, he never even thinks about it. He is content with these two things: acting justly in what he is doing now, and being satisfied with what is assigned to him now. He lays aside all distracting and busy pursuits, and wants nothing else than to travel the straight road by way of the law, and, by traveling that straight road, to follow God.

12. What need is there for suspicious fear, when it is in your power to find out what ought to be done? If you see clearly, go that way contentedly, without turning back. If you do not see clearly, stop and consult the best advisers. And if other things stand against you, go on as far as your powers allow, with careful thought, keeping to what seems just. For it is best to achieve what is just; and if you do fail, let your failure be in attempting it. Whoever follows reason in everything is calm and active at the same time, and also cheerful and composed.

13. As soon as you wake from sleep, ask yourself whether it will make any difference to you if someone else does what is just and right. It will make no difference. You have not forgotten, I suppose, those who put on arrogant airs as they hand out praise or blame to others: what they are like in bed and at table. Nor have you forgotten what they do, what they avoid and what they pursue, and how they steal and how they rob, not with hands and feet, but with the most precious part of themselves. For by that part, when a person chooses, there come into being faithfulness, modesty, truth, law, and a good divine spirit within, which is to say, happiness.

14. To nature, who gives all things and takes them all back, the person who is educated and modest says: "Give what you will; take back what you will." And he says it not proudly, but obediently, and well pleased with her.

15. Little of your life is left. Live as if on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether someone lives there or here, if everywhere he lives in the world as in one city, one political community. Let people see, let them come to know, a true human being who lives in keeping with nature. If they cannot bear him, let them kill him. For that is better than to live as they do.
16. No longer talk at all about what kind of person a good person ought to be; be one.

17. Constantly keep in view the whole of time and the whole of matter, and consider that every individual thing, measured in matter, is a fig seed, and measured in time, a single turn of a hand drill.
18. Look at everything that exists, and notice that it is already breaking up and changing, rotting, as it were, or scattering; or notice that everything is formed by nature to die.

19. Consider what people are like when they are eating, sleeping, having sex, relieving themselves, and so on. Then consider what they are like when they are domineering and arrogant, or angry and scolding from their high position. Yet a short time ago, how many masters they were slaves to, and for what things! And consider what condition they will be in a little while from now.
20. Whatever the nature of the universe brings to each thing is for that thing's good. And it is for its good at the very time that nature brings it.

21. "The earth loves the rain," and "the solemn sky loves"; and the universe loves to make whatever is going to be. So I say to the universe: I love as you love. And is this not also what we mean when we say that this or that "loves" to happen, that is, usually happens?

22. Either you go on living here, and you are used to it by now; or you are going away, and that was your own will; or you are dying, and you have done your duty. Besides these, there is nothing. So take heart.

23. Always keep it clear to yourself that this piece of land is like any other, and that everything here is the same as on a mountaintop, or on the seashore, or wherever you choose to be. For you will find just what Plato says: living within the walls of a city as in a shepherd's fold on a mountain.

24. What is my ruling faculty to me now? What kind of thing am I making it now? What am I using it for now? Is it empty of understanding? Is it cut loose and torn away from life in community with others? Is it so melted into and mixed with this poor flesh that it moves along with it?

25. Someone who runs away from his master is a runaway. But the law is a master, and whoever breaks the law is a runaway. And whoever is grieved, or angry, or afraid is dissatisfied because something has happened, or is happening, or will happen, among the things appointed by the one who rules all things. And he is Law, and he assigns to each person what is fitting. So whoever is afraid, or grieved, or angry is a runaway.

26. A man deposits seed in a womb and goes away; then another cause takes it over, works on it, and makes a child. What a thing, from such material! Again, the child passes food down its throat; then another cause takes it over and makes perception and movement, and in short, life and strength and other things besides. How many they are, and how strange! Look, then, at the things that are produced in so hidden a way, and see the power at work, just as we see the power that carries things downward and upward: not with our eyes, but no less plainly.

27. Constantly consider how everything, just as it is now, was the same in times past too; and consider that it will be the same again. Set before your eyes whole plays and whole stages of the same pattern, whatever you know from your own experience or from older history: for example, the whole court of Hadrianus, the whole court of Antoninus, and the whole court of Philippus, of Alexander, of Croesus. For all those were plays just like the ones we see now, only with different actors.

28. Picture everyone who is grieved or discontented at anything as being like a pig at the sacrifice, kicking and squealing. Like that pig, too, is the person who lies on his bed and silently laments the bonds that hold us. And consider that only to the rational being is it given to follow willingly what happens; simply to follow is a necessity laid on all.
29. With each thing you do, one at a time, stop and ask yourself whether death is something terrible because it deprives you of this.

30. When someone's fault offends you, turn at once to yourself and consider how you go wrong in a similar way: for example, in thinking that money is a good thing, or pleasure, or a bit of reputation, and so on. For if you attend to this, and also add the thought that he is under compulsion—for what else could he do?—you will quickly forget your anger. Or, if you are able, take the compulsion away from him.

31. When you have seen Satyron the Socratic, think of either Eutyches or Hymen; when you have seen Euphrates, think of Eutychion or Silvanus; when you have seen Alciphron, think of Tropaeophorus; when you have seen Xenophon, think of Crito or Severus; and when you have looked at yourself, think of any one of the other Caesars. Do the same in the case of everyone. Then let this thought be in your mind: where are those men now? Nowhere, or nobody knows where. For in this way you will keep seeing human things as smoke and nothing at all, especially if you reflect at the same time that what has once changed will never exist again in all the endless span of time. And you: how brief is the span of your existence? Why are you not content to pass through this short time in an orderly way? What material and what opportunity for your own activity are you running away from? For what else are all these things but exercises for reason, once it has looked carefully and searchingly into the nature of the things that happen in life? Keep at it, then, until you have made these things your own, as a strong stomach makes everything its own, as a blazing fire makes flame and light out of whatever is thrown into it.

32. Do not let anyone be able to say truthfully of you that you are not simple or that you are not good. Let anyone who thinks anything of the kind about you be a liar. And this is entirely in your power. For who can stop you from being good and simple? Only decide to live no longer if you are not such a person. For reason does not allow you to live if you are not.

33. In the material we have to work with, our life, what can be done or said in the way most in keeping with reason? Whatever it is, you have the power to do it or say it; do not make excuses that you are prevented. You will not stop lamenting until your mind is in this condition: that doing what fits the constitution of a human being, in whatever material is set before you and put in your hands, is to you what luxury is to lovers of pleasure. For a person ought to count as enjoyment everything he has the power to do in keeping with his own nature. And he has that power everywhere. A cylinder is not given the power to move everywhere by its own motion; nor is water, nor fire, nor anything else governed by nature or by a soul without reason. For the things that check them and stand in their way are many. But intelligence and reason can make their way through everything that opposes them, in whatever way they are formed by nature and as they choose. Set before your eyes this ease with which reason will be carried through all things, as fire is carried upward, a stone downward, a cylinder down a slope, and look for nothing further. For all other obstacles either affect only the body, which is a dead thing; or else they do not crush us or do any harm of any kind, except through opinion and through reason itself giving way. For if they did harm us, whoever felt that harm would at once become bad. Now with all other things that have a certain constitution, whatever harm happens to any of them, the thing so affected is made worse by it. But in the same situation a human being becomes better, if one may say so, and more worthy of praise, by making right use of what befalls him. And finally, remember that nothing harms someone who is truly a citizen unless it harms the state; and nothing harms the state unless it harms law, that is, order. And of the things called misfortunes, not one harms law. So what does not harm law harms neither state nor citizen.

34. For someone who has taken true principles deep into himself, even the briefest saying, any commonplace one, is enough to remind him to be free from grief and fear. For example: "Leaves, some the wind scatters on the ground; so is the race of men." Your children, too, are leaves. Leaves too are those who shout as if they deserved to be believed and hand out praise, or on the other hand curse, or blame and sneer in secret. And leaves, in the same way, are those who will receive a person's fame and pass it on to later times. For all such things "come forth in the season of spring," as the poet says; then the wind throws them down; then the forest puts out other leaves in their place. A brief existence is common to all things; and yet you run from everything and chase after everything as if it would last forever. A little while, and you will close your eyes; and soon someone else will mourn the one who saw you to your grave.

35. The healthy eye ought to see everything visible and not say, "I want green things"; for that is the condition of a diseased eye. The healthy sense of hearing and of smell ought to be ready to perceive everything that can be heard and smelled. The healthy stomach ought to take all food as a mill takes everything it is made to grind. And so the healthy mind ought to be ready for everything that happens. But the mind that says, "Let my dear children live," and "Let everyone praise whatever I do," is an eye looking for green things, or teeth looking for soft things.

36. No one is so fortunate that, when he is dying, there will not be some people standing by who are glad of what is about to happen. Suppose he was a good and wise man: will there not be at least someone who says to himself, "At last we can breathe freely, rid of this schoolmaster. It is true that he was harsh to none of us, but I could tell that he silently condemned us"? That is what is said of a good man. But in our own case, how many other reasons are there for which many people want to be rid of us? So consider this when you are dying, and you will leave more contentedly by thinking: "I am going away from a life in which even my companions, for whom I have struggled so hard, prayed so much and cared so much, themselves want me gone, hoping perhaps to gain some small advantage from it." Why, then, should anyone cling to a longer stay here? Yet do not, for this reason, go away less kindly disposed toward them. Keep your own character: stay friendly, well-meaning and gentle. And on the other hand, do not go as though you were being torn away. When someone dies a quiet death, the poor soul slips easily out of the body; your departure from people ought to be like that. For nature joined you to them and made you their companion. But is she now undoing that bond? Very well: I am parted from them as from my kin, not dragged away resisting, but going without compulsion. For this too is one of the things that are in keeping with nature.
37. Train yourself, as far as possible, whenever anyone does anything, to ask yourself: "What is this person's purpose in doing this?" But begin with yourself, and examine yourself first.

38. Remember that what pulls the strings is the thing hidden within. That is the power of persuasion; that is life; that, if one may say so, is the human being. When you think about yourself, never include the vessel that surrounds you and the instruments attached to it. For they are like an axe, differing only in this: that they grow on the body. Indeed, without the cause that moves them and holds them back, these parts are of no more use than the weaver's shuttle, the writer's pen, or the driver's whip.

chapters.title: Book 11
paragraphs: 1. These are the marks of the rational soul. It sees itself, examines itself, and makes itself whatever it chooses to be. It enjoys the fruit it bears itself—whereas the fruits of plants, and whatever in animals corresponds to fruit, are enjoyed by others. It reaches its own goal wherever the limit of life is set. It is not like a dance or a play or anything of that kind, where the whole performance is left incomplete if something cuts it short. In every part, and wherever it is stopped, it makes what was set before it full and complete, so that it can say: I have what is my own. Further, it travels through the whole universe and the empty space around it, and surveys its shape. It reaches out into the endlessness of time, and grasps and understands the periodic renewal of all things. It understands that those who come after us will see nothing new, and that those who came before us saw nothing more. In a way, a person of forty, if he has any understanding at all, has seen everything that has been and everything that will be, because all things are so uniform. This too is a mark of the rational soul: love of one's neighbor, truthfulness and modesty, and valuing nothing more highly than itself. Valuing nothing more highly than itself is also a mark of law. So right reason and the reason that belongs to justice do not differ at all.

2. You will think little of delightful singing, of dancing, and of the pancratium—the all-in fighting contest—if you break the melody down into its separate notes and ask yourself of each one, "Is this what overpowers me?" You will be too ashamed to admit that it does. Do the same with dancing, at each movement and each pose; and the same with the pancratium. In everything, then, except virtue and the acts that come from virtue, remember to break things down into their separate parts, and by dividing them in this way come to think little of them. Apply the same method to your whole life too.

3. What a soul that is which is ready, if at any moment it must be separated from the body, to be extinguished, or scattered, or to go on existing! But this readiness must come from a person's own judgment, not from mere obstinacy, as with the Christians. It must be thought through and dignified, and such that it could persuade someone else, without any theatrical display.
4. Have I done something for the common good? Then I have had my reward. Keep this always before your mind, and never stop doing such good.
5. What is your craft? To be good. And how is this done well, except by means of general principles—some about the nature of the universe, and others about how a human being is properly made?

6. At first, tragedies were put on the stage to remind people of the things that happen to them. They reminded people that it is according to nature for things to happen this way, and that if what is shown on the stage delights you, you should not be distressed by what happens on the larger stage. For you see that these things must turn out this way, and that even those who cry out "O Cithaeron!" have to bear them. And the dramatists do say some things well, especially this: "If the gods neglect me and my children, this too has its reason." And again: "We must not chafe and fret at what happens." And: "Reap life's harvest like the ripe ear of wheat." And other things of the same kind. After tragedy came the Old Comedy. It spoke with the frankness of a teacher, and its very bluntness was useful in reminding people to beware of arrogance; for this purpose Diogenes, too, used to borrow from these writers. But as for the Middle Comedy that came next, consider what it was like; and then consider for what purpose the New Comedy was brought in, which little by little sank into mere skill at imitation. Everyone knows that even these writers say some good things. But the whole design of this kind of poetry and drama—what is it aiming at?
7. How plain it is that no other condition of life is so well suited to philosophy as the one you happen to be in now!

8. A branch cut off from the branch next to it is necessarily cut off from the whole tree as well. In the same way, a person separated from another person has fallen away from the whole community. A branch is cut off by someone else. But a person separates himself from his neighbor by his own act, when he hates him and turns away from him; and he does not realize that he has at the same time cut himself off from the whole body of society. Yet Zeus, who founded this community, has certainly given us this privilege: it is in our power to grow back onto what is next to us, and to become once more a part that helps make up the whole. But if this kind of separation happens often, it becomes hard for the part that breaks away to be united again and restored to what it was. Finally, the branch that grew together with the tree from the start, and has always shared one life with it, is not like a branch that was cut off and then grafted back on. Gardeners say something like this of a grafted branch: that it grows along with the rest of the tree, but is not of one mind with it.

9. When you are going forward in keeping with right reason, those who try to stand in your way will not be able to turn you aside from acting rightly. So do not let them drive you from your kindly feeling toward them either. Guard both equally: not only steadiness in judgment and action, but also gentleness toward those who try to hinder you or trouble you in any other way. For it is a weakness to resent them, just as it is a weakness to be turned from your course of action and to give in out of fear. Both are deserters from their post alike: the one who gives in out of fear, and the one who becomes estranged from someone who is by nature his kinsman and friend.

10. No nature is inferior to craft, for the crafts imitate the natures of things. If this is so, then the nature that is the most perfect of all natures, and the one that contains them all, cannot fall short of the skill of any craft. Now all the crafts make the lesser things for the sake of the higher; so the nature of the universe does this too. And this ordering is where justice has its origin, and the other virtues have their foundation in justice. For justice will not be kept if we care about the in-between things that are neither good nor bad, or if we are easily deceived, careless and changeable.

11. Your chasing after certain things, or running from them, disturbs you. If those things do not come to you, still, in a way, it is you who go to them. So let your judgment about them be at rest, and they will stay quiet, and you will not be seen chasing after them or running from them.

12. The soul keeps its shape as a sphere when it neither reaches out toward anything, nor shrinks inward, nor scatters, nor sinks down, but is lit by the light by which it sees the truth—the truth of all things and the truth within itself.

13. Suppose someone despises me. That is his concern. My concern is not to be found doing or saying anything that deserves contempt. Will someone hate me? That is his concern. But I will be gentle and kind toward everyone, and ready to show even that person his mistake—not reproachfully, nor as if showing off my patience, but nobly and honestly, like the great Phocion, unless he was only pretending. For that is how one ought to be within: a person should be seen by the gods neither discontented about anything nor complaining. For what is bad for you, if you are now doing what suits your own nature, and are content with what at this moment suits the nature of the universe? For you are a human being placed at your post so that the common good may be achieved in one way or another.
14. People despise one another and flatter one another; they want to rise above one another, and they grovel before one another.

15. How rotten and false is the person who says, "I have decided to deal fairly with you!" What are you doing, man? There is no need to announce this. It will soon show itself in what you do. What your voice says ought to be plainly written on your forehead. Whatever a person's character is, it shows at once in his eyes, just as someone who is loved reads everything at once in the eyes of those who love him. The honest, good person ought to be exactly like someone who smells strongly, so that anyone who comes near him must smell it at once, whether he wants to or not. But a show of straightforwardness is like a crooked stick. Nothing is more shameful than the friendship of a wolf—false friendship. Avoid this above all. The good, the straightforward and the kind show all this in their eyes, and there is no mistaking it.

16. The power to live in the best way lies in the soul, if it is indifferent to things that are indifferent. And it will be indifferent to them if it looks at each of these things by itself and at all of them together, and if it remembers that none of them produces in us an opinion about itself, and none of them comes to us. They stay where they are, unmoving; it is we who produce the judgments about them and, so to speak, write them in ourselves. It is in our power not to write them; and if such judgments have slipped into our minds without our noticing, it is in our power to wipe them out. And it will be indifferent if we remember, too, that we need to give things such attention only for a short time, and then life will be over. Besides, what is so hard about doing this? If the things themselves are in keeping with nature, take pleasure in them, and they will be easy for you. But if they are against nature, look for what suits your own nature and press on toward it, even if it brings you no fame; for everyone is allowed to seek his own good.
17. Consider where each thing has come from, what it is made of, what it changes into, what it will be like once it has changed, and that it will come to no harm.

18. If someone has wronged you, consider first: what is my relation to other people? We are made for one another; and, in another respect, I was made to be set over them, as a ram over the flock or a bull over the herd. But go back to first principles, and start from this: if it is not true that all things are mere atoms, then it is nature that orders all things. If that is so, the lower things exist for the sake of the higher, and the higher for the sake of one another. Second, consider what sort of people they are at table, in bed, and so on; and above all, what compulsions their opinions put them under; and as for their acts, consider with what pride they do what they do. Third, if they are doing right, we ought not to be displeased. If they are not doing right, it is plain that they do wrong against their will and out of ignorance. For just as every soul is deprived of the truth against its will, so too it is deprived against its will of the power to treat each person as he deserves. That is why people are pained when they are called unjust, ungrateful, greedy—in a word, wrongdoers toward their neighbors. Fourth, consider that you yourself do many things wrong, and that you are a human being like the others. Even if you keep from certain faults, you still have the tendency to commit them, though you keep from them out of cowardice, or concern for your reputation, or some other such petty motive. Fifth, consider that you do not even understand whether they are doing wrong or not, for many things are done with an eye to circumstances. In short, a person has to learn a great deal before he can judge another person's acts correctly. Sixth, when you are deeply resentful or upset, consider that human life lasts only a moment, and after a short while we are all laid out dead. Seventh, it is not people's acts that disturb us, since those acts are rooted in their own ruling faculties; it is our own opinions that disturb us. So take away these opinions: resolve to let go of your judgment that the act is something terrible, and your anger is gone. How, then, shall I take away these opinions? By reflecting that no wrong act of another person brings shame on you. For if anything besides what is shameful is bad, then you too must inevitably do many wrongs, and become a robber and everything else. Eighth, consider how much more pain we suffer from the anger and resentment such acts cause us than from the acts themselves that we are angry and resentful about. Ninth, consider that a kindly disposition is invincible, if it is genuine and not a forced smile or an act. For what can even the most violent person do to you if you go on being kind to him, and, when the chance comes, gently advise him and calmly set him right at the very moment he is trying to harm you? Say to him: "No, my child; we were made by nature for something else. I shall certainly not be harmed; it is you who are harming yourself, my child." And show him, gently and tactfully and by general principles, that this is so, and that not even bees behave as he does, nor any animals that nature has made to live in herds. You must do this without any hidden meaning and without reproach, but with affection and with no bitterness in your soul; not as if you were lecturing him, nor so that some bystander may admire you, but either when he is alone, and if others are present . . . Remember these nine rules as if you had received them as a gift from the Muses, and begin at last to be a human being while you are still alive. But you must avoid flattering people just as much as resenting them, for both set us against others and lead to harm. And when anger stirs, keep this truth at hand: to be carried away by passion is not manly. Gentleness and mildness, just as they are more in keeping with human nature, are also more manly. Whoever has these qualities has strength, nerve and courage—not the person who is given to fits of passion and discontent. For the closer a mind comes to freedom from passion, the closer it comes to strength. And just as feeling pain is a sign of weakness, so is anger. For whoever gives in to pain and whoever gives in to anger are both wounded, and both have surrendered. And if you like, accept a tenth gift too, from Apollo, the leader of the Muses: to expect bad people not to do wrong is madness, for whoever expects this wants the impossible. But to let them behave like this toward others, and expect them not to wrong you, is unreasonable and tyrannical.

19. There are four chief ways in which the ruling faculty goes astray. Be constantly on guard against them, and when you catch them, wipe them out, saying each time: "This thought is not necessary." "This one tends to break the bonds of community." "What you are about to say does not come from your real thoughts"—and you should count it among the most absurd things for a person not to speak from his real thoughts. The fourth is when you reproach yourself for anything. For this shows that the more divine part in you has been overpowered and has given way to the less honorable and perishable part, the body, and to its coarse pleasures.

20. The airy part of you, and all the fiery parts mixed in you, tend upward by nature; yet in obedience to the ordering of the universe they are held down here in the compound mass of the body. And the whole of the earthy part in you, and the watery part, though they tend downward, are still raised up and hold a position that is not natural to them. In this way even the elements obey the whole: once they have been set in any place, they are forced to stay there until the whole sounds the signal for them to break up again. Is it not strange, then, that only your intelligent part should be disobedient and discontented with its place? And yet nothing is imposed on it by force; only what is in keeping with its nature is imposed on it. Still it does not submit, but is carried the opposite way. For the impulse toward injustice, self-indulgence, anger, grief and fear is nothing but the act of one who is turning away from nature. And when the ruling faculty is discontented with anything that happens, it too deserts its post. For it was made for piety and reverence toward the gods no less than for justice. Piety and reverence, too, come under the general heading of contentment with the way things are ordered; and indeed they are prior to acts of justice.

21. Someone who does not have one aim in life, always the same, cannot be one and the same person all through his life. But what I have said is not enough unless I add what that aim ought to be. Most people regard many things as good, in one way or another; but people do not hold the same opinion about all of them, only about certain things, namely the things that concern the common interest. In the same way, we ought to set ourselves an aim that is shared and civic—one that serves the community. For whoever directs all his own efforts toward this aim will make all his acts consistent, and so will always be the same.
22. Think of the country mouse and the town mouse, and of the town mouse's alarm and panic.
23. Socrates used to call the opinions of the many "Lamiae"—bogeys to frighten children.
24. The Lacedaemonians—the Spartans—at their public shows, used to set out seats in the shade for strangers, but sat down anywhere themselves.

25. Socrates excused himself to Perdiccas for not going to visit him, saying: "It is because I do not want to perish by the worst of all ends: that is, I do not want to receive a favor and then be unable to return it."
26. In the writings of the Ephesians there was this rule: to keep constantly in mind one or another of the people of old who practiced virtue.

27. The Pythagoreans tell us to look at the sky in the morning, so that we are reminded of those bodies that always do the same things and do their work in the same way, and are reminded too of their purity and their nakedness. For no star wears a veil.

28. Think what kind of man Socrates was when he wrapped himself in an animal skin, after Xanthippe had taken his cloak and gone out; and what Socrates said to his friends who were ashamed of him and drew back from him when they saw him dressed like that.
29. In writing and in reading you will not be able to lay down rules for others until you have first learned to follow rules yourself. Much more is this true in life.
30. You are a slave: free speech is not for you.
31. As Homer says in the Odyssey: "And my heart laughed within me."
32. As Hesiod says in the Works and Days: "And they will curse virtue, speaking harsh words."
33. To look for a fig in winter is the act of a madman; and the person who looks for his child when the child is no longer granted to him is just like him. So Epictetus says.

34. When a person kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should whisper to himself: "Tomorrow, perhaps, you will die." "But," someone objects, "those are words of ill omen." "No word is ill-omened," said Epictetus, "that speaks of any work of nature. Or if it is, then it is also ill-omened to speak of ears of grain being harvested."
35. The unripe grape, the ripe bunch, the dried grape: all are changes, not into nothing, but into something that does not yet exist. So Epictetus says.
36. No one can rob us of our free will, as Epictetus says.

37. Epictetus also said that a person must find a method, a set of rules, for giving assent—for deciding which impressions to agree to. As for his impulses, he must take care that they take account of circumstances, that they serve the common good, and that they take account of the worth of the thing they aim at. He should keep away from sensual desire altogether; and he should feel aversion toward none of the things that are not in our power.
38. So, he said, the dispute is not about some ordinary matter, but about whether we are to be mad or not.

39. Socrates used to ask: "What do you want: the souls of rational beings, or of irrational ones?"—"Of rational beings."—"Rational beings of what kind: sound or unsound?"—"Sound."—"Then why do you not seek them?"—"Because we have them."—"Then why do you fight and quarrel?"

chapters.title: Book 12
paragraphs: 1. All the things you hope to reach by a roundabout road, you can have now, if you do not refuse them to yourself. And not refusing them means this: paying no attention to all that is past, entrusting the future to providence, and directing the present only by piety and justice. By piety, so that you are content with the lot you have been given, for nature made it for you and you for it. By justice, so that you always speak the truth freely and without disguise, and do what is in keeping with the law and with the worth of each. And do not let yourself be held back by another person's wickedness, or by what people think or say, or even by the sensations of the poor flesh that has grown around you; the part that suffers those sensations will see to that. Whenever the time comes for you to depart, if you let everything else go and honor only your ruling faculty and the divine spirit within you, and if you are afraid, not because you must one day stop living, but of never having begun to live according to nature—then you will be a man worthy of the universe that brought you into being. You will stop being a stranger in your own native land. You will stop marveling at what happens every day as if it were something unexpected, and stop depending on this thing or that.

2. God sees the ruling faculties of all people stripped bare of their material wrappings, their husks and their impurities. For with his own mind alone he touches only the intelligence that has flowed from himself into these bodies. If you train yourself to look at people this way too, you will free yourself from a great deal of trouble. For someone who pays no attention to the poor flesh that wraps him will surely not trouble himself with clothes and houses and fame, and with outward things like these and all their show.

3. There are three things you are made of: a little body, a little breath, and intelligence. The first two are yours only in the sense that you have a duty to take care of them; the third alone is truly your own. Suppose, then, that you separate from yourself—that is, from your understanding—all of these: whatever others do or say; whatever you yourself have done or said; whatever troubles you about the future because it might happen; whatever, in the body that wraps you or in the breath that nature joined to the body, clings to you without your choosing; and whatever is swept around by the whirling current outside you. And suppose you do this so that the power of your mind, set free from what fate controls, can live pure and free by itself, doing what is just, accepting what happens, and speaking the truth. If, I repeat, you separate from this ruling faculty everything that has clung to it through the impressions of the senses, and everything in the time to come and in the time that is past; if you make yourself like the sphere of Empedocles, "round on every side, resting in its joyful rest"; and if you try to live only the life that is truly yours, which is the present—then you will be able to live the rest of your life, until you die, free from disturbance, nobly, and obedient to the divine spirit within you.

4. I have often wondered how it is that each person loves himself more than all the rest of humanity, and yet cares less about his own opinion of himself than about other people's opinion of him. Suppose a god or a wise teacher stood beside someone and told him not to think or plan anything that he would not say out loud the moment he thought it. He could not bear it for a single day. That is how much more we care about what our neighbors will think of us than about what we will think of ourselves.

5. How can it be that the gods, who have arranged everything well and with kindness toward human beings, have overlooked this one thing? Some people are very good people, who have had, we might say, the closest fellowship with the divine, and through devout acts and religious rites have been on the most intimate terms with it. How can it be that once such people die, they never exist again, but are completely extinguished? But if that is so, be sure that if it ought to have been otherwise, the gods would have made it otherwise. For if it were just, it would also be possible; and if it were in keeping with nature, nature would have brought it about. So since it is not so—if in fact it is not—be convinced that it ought not to have been. For you can see for yourself that in raising this question you are arguing with God. And we would not argue this way with the gods unless they were supremely good and supremely just. But if they are, they would not have let anything in the ordering of the universe be neglected unjustly or without reason.

6. Practice even the things you despair of ever mastering. For the left hand is clumsy at everything else for lack of practice, yet it holds the reins more firmly than the right, because it has been trained to do that.

7. Consider what condition, in body and in soul, a person should be in when death overtakes him. And consider how short life is, the endless gulf of time behind us and ahead of us, and the frailty of all matter.

8. Look at the forms of things, stripped of their coverings. Look at the purposes behind actions. Consider what pain is, what pleasure is, what death is, and what fame is. Consider who is the cause of his own unrest; how no one is ever hindered by anyone else; and that everything is opinion.

9. In putting your principles into practice, you must be like the all-in fighter, the pancratiast, and not like the gladiator. The gladiator drops the sword he uses and is killed. But the fighter always has his hand, and needs to do nothing but use it.
10. See what things are in themselves, by dividing them into their matter, their form, and their purpose.
11. What power a human being has: to do nothing except what God will approve, and to accept everything that God may give him.

12. When something happens in keeping with nature, we should blame neither the gods, for they do no wrong either willingly or unwillingly, nor human beings, for they do no wrong except unwillingly. So we should blame no one.
13. How ridiculous, and what a stranger, is the person who is surprised at anything that happens in life!

14. Either there is a necessity of fate and an order that nothing can break, or a kind providence, or a confusion without purpose and without anyone directing it. If there is a necessity that nothing can break, why do you resist? If there is a providence that can be won over, make yourself worthy of help from the divine. And if there is a confusion with no one governing it, be content that in such a storm you have within you an intelligence that governs. Even if the storm sweeps you away, let it sweep away the poor flesh, the poor breath, and everything else; the intelligence, at least, it will not sweep away.
15. Does the light of a lamp go on shining, without losing its brightness, until it is put out? And will the truth in you, and your justice and self-control, be put out before you die?

16. When someone seems to have done wrong, say to yourself: How do I even know that this was a wrong? And even if he has done wrong, how do I know that he has not already condemned himself? That would be like tearing at his own face. Consider that someone who does not want a bad person to do wrong is like someone who does not want the fig tree to put juice in its figs, or babies to cry, or horses to neigh, or anything else to happen that must happen. What else can a person with such a character do? So if you are irritable, cure this man's character.
17. If it is not right, do not do it. If it is not true, do not say it. For let your effort be—

18. In every case, always look at what it is that produces the impression in you. Take it apart by dividing it into its form, its matter, its purpose, and the length of time within which it must come to an end.

19. Realize at last that you have something in you better and more divine than the things that stir up your passions and jerk you about, as if on strings. What is in my mind at this moment? Is it fear, or suspicion, or desire, or something of that kind?
20. First, do nothing thoughtlessly or without a purpose. Second, let your actions aim at nothing but the common good.

21. Consider that before long you will be no one and nowhere. And none of the things you now see will exist, nor any of the people now alive. For everything is made by nature to change, to be transformed and to perish, so that other things may come to be, one after another in unbroken succession.

22. Consider that everything is opinion, and your opinion is in your power. So take away your opinion whenever you choose. Then, like a sailor who has rounded the headland, you will find calm, everything settled, and a bay without a wave.

23. Any single activity, whatever it is, suffers nothing bad from having stopped, if it stops at its proper time. Nor does the person who did it suffer anything bad just because the activity has stopped. In the same way, then, the whole made up of all our acts—which is our life—suffers nothing bad from having stopped, if it stops at its proper time. Nor has the person who brought this series to an end at its proper time been badly treated. The proper time and the limit are set by nature: sometimes by a person's own nature, as in old age, but always by the nature of the universe, whose parts, by changing, keep the whole universe forever young and complete. And whatever benefits the whole is always good and always in season. So the end of life is not bad for anyone, because it is not shameful: it does not depend on our choice, and it is not against the common good. And it is good, since it comes in its season, benefits the whole, and fits in with it. For in this way, too, whoever moves in the same way as God, and in his mind moves toward the same ends, is moved by God.

24. You must have these three principles ready to hand. First, in what you do, do nothing thoughtlessly, or in any way other than justice herself would act. And as for what happens to you from outside, remember that it happens either by chance or by providence; and you must neither blame chance nor accuse providence. Second, consider what each living being is, from the seed until it receives a soul, and from the time it receives a soul until it gives that soul back; and consider what things each being is made of, and into what things it is broken up. Third, suppose you were suddenly lifted up above the earth, and looked down on human affairs, and saw how great their variety is. And suppose that at the same time you saw at a glance how great a multitude of beings live all around, in the air and in the ether. Then consider that however often you were lifted up, you would see the same things: sameness of form and shortness of duration. Are these things to be proud of?
25. Throw away opinion, and you are saved. Who, then, is stopping you from throwing it away?

26. When you are troubled by anything, you have forgotten these things. You have forgotten that everything happens according to the nature of the universe. You have forgotten that another person's wrongdoing is nothing to you. You have forgotten, too, that everything that happens has always happened this way, will always happen this way, and is happening this way everywhere now. You have forgotten how close the kinship is between each person and the whole human race: it is a community not of a little blood or seed, but of intelligence. You have forgotten, too, that each person's intelligence is a god, and has flowed from God. You have forgotten that nothing is anyone's own, but that his child, his body and his very soul came from God. You have forgotten that everything is opinion. And lastly, you have forgotten that each person lives only the present moment, and loses only that.

27. Keep calling to mind those who complained bitterly about something; those who stood out most for their great fame, or their misfortunes, or their feuds, or their fortunes of any kind. Then ask: where are they all now? Smoke and ash and a story—or not even a story. And bring to mind every case of this kind: how Fabius Catellinus lived in the country, and Lucius Lupus in his gardens, and Stertinius at Baiae, and Tiberius on Capreae, and Velius Rufus (or Rufus at Velia). In short, think of all the proud, eager chasing after things. Think how worthless everything is that people strain so hard for. And think how much more truly philosophical it is for a person to show himself, in whatever opportunities come to him, just, self-controlled and obedient to the gods, and to do this with complete simplicity. For pride that prides itself on having no pride is the most unbearable pride of all.

28. To those who ask, "Where have you seen the gods, or how do you know that they exist, that you worship them?" I answer: first, they can be seen, even with the eyes. Second, I have never seen my own soul either, and yet I honor it. So it is with the gods: from what I constantly experience of their power, I understand that they exist, and I revere them.

29. What keeps life safe and sound is this: to look into each thing through and through, and see what it is in itself—what its matter is, and what its form is; and with all your soul to do what is just and to speak the truth. What is left, then, but to enjoy life, joining one good thing to the next, so as to leave not even the smallest gap between them?

30. There is one light of the sun, even though it is broken up by walls, mountains and countless other things. There is one common substance, even though it is divided among countless bodies, each with its own qualities. There is one soul, even though it is divided among countless natures and separate individuals. There is one intelligent soul, even though it seems to be divided. Now, among the things just mentioned, all the other parts, such as air and matter, have no sensation and no fellowship with one another. Yet even these parts are held together by the intelligent principle, and by the weight that draws them toward the same place. But the mind, in its own special way, reaches out toward whatever is of its own kind and joins with it; and its longing for fellowship is never broken off.

31. What do you want? To go on existing? Well then, do you want to feel, to have impulses, to grow and then to stop growing, to use your voice, to think? Which of all these things seems to you worth wanting? But if all these things are easy to think little of, turn to what is left: to follow reason and God. But it does not fit with honoring reason and God to be troubled that death will take the other things away from a person.

32. How tiny a part of boundless, bottomless time is given to each person! For it is very soon swallowed up in eternity. And how tiny a part of the whole of substance; how tiny a part of the soul of the universe; and on what a tiny clod of the whole earth you crawl! Reflecting on all this, think nothing great except this: to act as your own nature leads you, and to bear what the common nature brings.
33. How does the ruling faculty make use of itself? Everything depends on this. Everything else, whether it is within your choice or not, is only dead ash and smoke.
34. This thought does more than any other to move us to think little of death: even those who believe pleasure is good and pain is bad have still looked down on death.

35. For the person who counts as good only what comes in its proper season; to whom it is all the same whether he has done more or fewer acts in keeping with right reason; and to whom it makes no difference whether he looks upon the world for a longer or a shorter time—for this person, death is not a terrible thing either.

36. Man, you have been a citizen in this great city, the world. What difference does it make to you whether it was for five years or for three? For what is in keeping with the laws is just for everyone. Where is the hardship, then, if it is not a tyrant or an unjust judge who sends you away from the city, but nature, who brought you into it? It is as if a praetor who had hired an actor were to dismiss him from the stage. "But I have not played all five acts, only three." You are right; but in life, three acts make the whole play. For what makes a play complete is decided by the one who once caused it to be put together and now causes it to be broken up; and you are the cause of neither. So leave contented, for the one who releases you is content too.
